articles.title: Gov. Josh Shapiro sails to a second term in battleground Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Shapiro, a possible 2028 Democratic presidential contender, defeated GOP state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro easily defeated Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity in his re-election bid, NBC News projects. Shapiro, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, did not face much competition from Garrity, who trailed by double digits in polls in the run-up to Election Day and was vastly outpaced in fundraising. “The picture is starting to come into focus,” Shapiro said in a victory speech on Tuesday. “This is a good night for our commonwealth. And, it’s looking like it could be a pretty good night for our country too.” The substantial victory in a key battleground gives Shapiro a springboard into a potential White House bid. In the closing weeks of the contest, he launched a federal political action committee, New Path PAC, his first official step into national politics, which his campaign said was done so he could help congressional candidates in his state. Shapiro enjoys solid approval ratings in his state, though voters are more mixed on whether he should seek the presidency. He spent much of the campaign seeking to boost downballot House candidates locked in much closer swing races, which could determine control of the chamber, as well as state legislators who could give Democrats full control in Harrisburg for the first time in more than 30 years. “With the way things are going tonight, I think I’m going to have plenty of ‘GSD’ [get s--- done] Democrats by my side ready to make more progress,” Shapiro said. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Garrity, meanwhile, struggled to break through in the race, and polling showed a large chunk of voters were unfamiliar with her candidacy. Republicans had cleared the field for her run ahead of the primary, seeking to avoid a messy fight that could distract from taking aim at Shapiro. In his victory address, Shapiro said Garrity called him and “wished me well and said she wants to work together to serve the people of Pennsylvania.” “Look, we have plenty of disagreements, that’s part of a healthy democracy,” he said. “And I appreciate her service to our commonwealth and our country.” In the closing weeks of the general election, Garrity sought to put some space between her and President Donald Trump over tariffs, outlining her differences with him in her only televised debate with Shapiro. The race was never particularly close, though the candidates did get into notable back-and-forths about data center policy, with Garrity coming out in favor of a moratorium, followed by Shapiro announcing new, tougher mandates for developers in the state.

articles.title: Paul Pelosi pleads no contest in California hit-and-run involving parked car
articles.summary: Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s husband struck a parked car in Northern California in July.
articles.body: Paul Pelosi, the husband of Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., pleaded no contest to a July hit-and-run involving a parked car and will have his driving privileges suspended for six months, a California prosecutor’s office said Tuesday. Pelosi, 86, pleaded no contest to misdemeanor hit-and-run and a traffic infraction of making an unlawful turn, the Napa County District Attorney’s Office said. Pelosi struck an unoccupied, parked vehicle in Yountville, a town in California’s wine country, on July 3 and left the scene, the prosecutor’s office said. He reached a plea agreement with prosecutors and was sentenced to one year of summary probation and is prohibited from driving for six months, the district attorney’s office said. Pelosi was also ordered to complete a 10-day work program, it said, and he paid $11,191.14 in restitution to the owner of the vehicle he hit. There were no allegations that drugs or alcohol were involved, and Pelosi was not arrested. A Pelosi family spokesperson previously told NBC News that Pelosi had “personally apologized” to the owner of the vehicle he hit and “assured them that he would take responsibility for the damage to their vehicle.” Nancy Pelosi, the former House speaker, is finishing her remaining term as a U.S. representative for her San Francisco-area district after a long tenure in Congress that began with a 1987 special election. Last year, she announced her retirement from Congress and said she would not seek re-election.

articles.title: Democrats score major Senate victory as Pappas defeats Trump-backed Republican in key battleground
articles.summary: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeats John Sununu in New Hampshire's high-stakes Senate race, a critical hold as Democrats seek the Senate majority.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk projects that Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will defeat former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu in a competitive and expensive swing state race. With 19.18% of the votes reported, Papas captured 60.6% compared to Sununu receiving 37.61% of the votes, according to Fox News Decision Desk. He will succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Pappas said his victory was not just for Democrats but for all of New Hampshire voters, saying the "broken status" is hurting everyone the same. "Tonight's results are a wake up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy," Pappas said. "For the cowards in Congress who have enabled health care cuts, tariffs and war and for the incompetent president who can't even be bothered to care how people are being heard." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee celebrated Pappas' victory, pointing to his previous service in the State House and the House of Representatives as proof that he is up for the job. "Chris has a proven bipartisan track record of doing what’s best for New Hampshire — and he’ll continue that fight in the Senate," the DSCC wrote on X. The victory by Pappas, a four-term congressman, is a boost for his party as the race was viewed as a must-hold for the Democrats as they try to win back the Senate majority from the GOP in the midterm elections. Sununu, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump but kept his distance from the president, was aiming to return to the U.S. Senate after 18 years away. Sununu repeatedly argued that Pappas had "been in Washington for 8 years and hasn't delivered for New Hampshire." "He has attempted very little in Congress. He's accomplished even less," Sununu told Fox News Digital recently. And he charged that Pappas would be "a rubber stamp for the far left." "I've worked across the aisle on fentanyl scheduling to make sure that fentanyl analogs are Schedule One and that we're able to stay ahead of the cartels and the drugs that they're pushing into this country. I challenged Joe Biden on the border." Pappas, a co-owner of the famed Puritan Backroom restaurant, which has been a family run business for over a century and is known for its chicken tenders and as a must-stop in Manchester for politicians, was elected to New Hampshire's five-member Executive Council before winning a seat in Congress. Pappas and Democrats repeatedly anchored Sununu to Trump, whose approval ratings are well underwater in New Hampshire and around the country. But Sununu told Fox News Digital, "This election is about New Hampshire. It's about who's going to give New Hampshire the strong independent voice we need in Washington, and that will be me...this is a six-year term. Donald Trump will be out of office in two years, and the question I have for voters is who's going to lead the country and the Senate in the right direction for New Hampshire." New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Ray Buckley also noted that Pappas' projected victory is historic because he is the first openly gay man to represent New Hampshire in the U.S. Senate. "Granite Staters know that Senator-elect Pappas will lead the fight for a freer, fairer future, and he will continue to deliver for our state," Buckley said. Pappas gave a special shutout to his husband during his victory speech, saying he was the luckiest guy because he is married to the man he loved. Sununu spent six years in the U.S. House before winning election to the Senate in 2002, defeating then-Gov. Jeanne Shaheen. But he lost his 2008 rematch with Shaheen. Sununu, served six years as governor before heading to Washington, D.C., as then-President George H.W. Bush's White House chief of staff. And one of his younger brothers, Chris Sununu, recently served eight years as governor before taking a break from politics. articles.title: Democrat Roy Cooper wins North Carolina Senate race, flipping seat from Republicans
articles.summary: It's the first time the state has elected a Democratic senator since 2008.
articles.body:
Democrat Roy Cooper has been projected to win a key Senate race in North Carolina, flipping a crucial seat previously held by Republican Thom Tillis, the BBC's news partner CBS reports.

Cooper is projected to beat Republican opponent Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee.

It's the first time the state will have elected a Democratic senator since 2008, in a major win for a party that is campaigning to win control of Congress from Republicans this midterm election.

Tillis announced his retirement from the Senate last year after falling out with President Donald Trump.

Follow live - US election results and analysis

US voters name economy and state of democracy as top issues, poll says

"You have made your voices heard and they were loud," Cooper told supporters in the state capital of Raleigh.

"For too many people in North Carolina, the middle class was feeling like a distant dream," while "the richest Americans were getting unimaginable wealth at our expense", he told the crowd.

"Today you said this has to stop," the Democrat added. "As your new United States Senator, I am ready to take that message to Washington and work to do something about it."

Before his Senate run, Cooper, 69, served as the governor of North Carolina from 2017 to 2025 and was previously the state's attorney general.

His campaign focused on lowering the cost of food and groceries, healthcare, energy and utilities, childcare, and housing.

Whatley, who was hand-picked by Trump for the Senate seat, had vowed to enact the president's agenda in the Senate, fight illegal immigration and roll back Democratic policies.

Tillis, North Carolina's outgoing senator, chose not to run for a third six-year term after voting against the president's domestic policy package - dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act - in a break from his Republican Party.

After the vote, Trump criticised Tillis and threatened to support other candidates in his re-election bid, calling him "a talker and complainer".

North Carolina's other sitting senator, Ted Budd, who was elected to his first six-year Senate term in 2023, is also a Republican.

articles.title: Trump-backed Byron Donalds to make history as Florida’s first Black governor
articles.summary: Byron Donalds makes history as the first Black Republican governor in the nation, defeating David Jolly in Florida's heated gubernatorial race.
articles.body: Rep. Byron Donalds just made history as the first Black politician to win a gubernatorial election in Florida as Fox News Decision Desk projected the congressman winning Tuesday's election. He is also the first Black Republican in the nation's history elected governor. Donalds, a three-term congressman from southwest Florida, defeated Democratic rival former Rep. David Jolly in a close race to win the Sunshine State's gubernatorial election, the Fox News Decision Desk projects. With his victory, the top House ally of President Donald Trump and MAGA champion with a growing national profile will succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis in steering the nation's third most populous state. "I am humbled and grateful beyond measure," Donalds said in a victory statement posted to X. "As your Governor, I will give you everything I have. We are going to make life in Florida more affordable. We are going to keep our streets safe. We are going to invest in our young people so that they can attain the Florida Dream that all of us love so dearly. Florida is the envy of the nation. I will fight day and night to keep it that way and to lift our state to even greater heights." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Continuing and building upon DeSantis' conservative agenda was a key part of Donalds' campaign for governor. Donalds was endorsed by Trump in February of last year, before he even formally launched his campaign for governor. Donalds declared his candidacy for governor during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Backed by Trump, Donalds won nearly half the vote in Florida's August GOP gubernatorial primary. He topped a crowded field of rivals that included Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner, and business executive James Fishback. Donalds made headlines in late September when some references to Trump, whose approval ratings have continued to decline, were scrubbed from his campaign website. A New York City native, Donalds moved to Florida to attend college. He worked in the finance, insurance, and banking fields before entering politics. A one-time Democrat, he became a Republican in 2010 amid the Tea Party movement. Donalds was elected to the Florida House in 2016, serving two terms before winning a seat in Congress. Jolly, a Florida native who served as a top advisor to then-Rep. Bill Young, also worked as a lawyer and a lobbyist before winning a special congressional election in March of 2014. He won a full two-year term to the House later that year before losing re-election in 2016. After leaving office he became a vocal Trump critic and a cable news political commentator. Jolly left the GOP in 2018 and became a Democrat last year before launching his gubernatorial campaign. During their showdown for governor, Donalds showcased anti-socialism messaging, repeatedly claiming that Jolly embraced "radical socialism." Firing back, Jolly told Fox News two weeks ago, "Byron Donalds is a liar. I've condemned socialism in the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] hundreds of times, and he knows that." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Florida was once the largest of the general election battlegrounds, but the state has shifted to the right over the past decade. DeSantis won his 2022 re-election by nearly 20 points and Trump carried the state by 13 points in his 2024 White House re-election victory. But despite Republicans enjoying a roughly 1.5 million registered voter advantage over the Democrats in the Sunshine State, Democrats are competitive again in Florida thanks to a rough political climate facing the GOP.

articles.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms will be Georgia’s next governor in historic win
articles.summary: Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades and the first Black wom...
articles.body:
Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia's top office in more than two decades and the first Black woman governor anywhere in the country.

Bottoms defeated her Republican opponent, healthcare executive Rick Jackson, who was endorsed by both outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp and President Donald Trump and who spent $200 million of his own money on the race.

The Associated Press called the race just before 9:30 p.m. Tuesday.

Bottoms will be the state's first Democratic governor since former Gov. Roy Barnes lost his bid for reelection in 2002. Republicans have had a grip on state government since Sonny Perdue won that election. Kemp has strong approval ratings but is term-limited and can't run again.

Bottoms, who served in the Biden administration after leaving city hall, ran a centrist campaign focused on pocketbook issues. In response to concerns over the massive growth of data centers and their impact on Georgians' power bills, Bottoms proposed a pause on their construction. She proposed a mechanism for local governments to cut taxes on groceries and basic household goods.

Medicaid expansion was central to her campaign, just as it had been for the Democratic nominees who preceded her. Bottoms framed it as a way for the state to fund more healthcare services and prevent further hospital closures.

With her win, Bottoms was able to accomplish what Democrat Stacey Abrams narrowly missed doing nearly a decade ago. Abrams was about 55,000 votes short of beating Kemp in 2018, and Georgia's statewide elections have been closely watched ever since.

But Bottoms' victory this year was far from certain. She and Jackson were neck and neck throughout the campaign, with Bottoms appearing to gain momentum as Election Day neared.

Both candidates attracted high-profile national figures to Georgia, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris who made appearances here during early voting to energize voters. On the Republican side, President Donald Trump visited the state twice during early voting, and other national Republicans like Sens. Rick Scott and Ted Cruz dropped in too in hopes of turning out conservative voters even as their chances of flipping Georgia's U.S. Senate seat seemed to slip away.

Bottoms' run for the governor's seat has been a bruising one. She faced an uphill battle against the millions of dollars Jackson spent flooding the airwaves with ads depicting her record as mayor as catastrophic for Atlanta. Scenes from 2020 flashed repeatedly on screens across the state, reminding voters of the Wendy's fast food restaurant and police cars that were set ablaze during protests in the wake of George Floyd's murder in Minnesota.

Jackson's campaign attempted to make Secoriea Turner, an 8-year-old Atlanta girl who was killed during those protests, an icon of Bottoms' alleged failures as mayor in spite of Turner's family's wishes .

Jackson's campaign also framed Bottoms' decision not to seek a second term in 2022 as her abandoning Atlanta at a difficult time, often repeating the line "bad mayors don't make good governors" on the campaign trail.

But in the last few weeks leading up to Election Day, Democrats in and outside of Georgia came to Bottoms' rescue. She raised about five times as much during the final reporting period as she did during the rest of her entire campaign, and in the last few days of the race, she received a $5 million boost from the Democratic Governors Association and another $2.5 million from former New York City mayor and Democratic presidential candidate Mike Bloomberg.

Kemp initially backed Jackson's rival in the GOP primary, but he has campaigned vigorously with Jackson in the general election, with the two men frequently seen together at rallies and campaign stops across the state. Kemp, who has maintained high approval ratings, has touted the state's economic strength and his administration's focus on tax cuts on the campaign trail, pitching Jackson as the best person to succeed him and continue moving Georgia on a similar path.

But the state's economy and population grew, so did concerns over the cost of living, which gave Bottoms and other down-ballot Democrats an opportunity to campaign on what consistently polled as voters' prevailing concern this year both nationally and here in Georgia.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

articles.title: GOP Rep. Tom Kean loses re-election bid after monthslong absence from Congress this year
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Democrat Rebecca Bennett has defeated Kean in his battleground New Jersey district.
articles.body: Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J., who faced criticism this year after a mysterious monthslong absence from Congress, was defeated by Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett, NBC News projects. Bennett’s victory over Kean, the son of New Jersey’s popular former GOP governor of the same name, was a key win for Democrats in their bid for the House majority. Kean, who was in his second term, had been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republicans on the ballot, and top super PACs yanked spending in support of Kean in the closing weeks of the campaign. He was absent from Capitol Hill from March 5 to June 30, when he revealed that he had been hospitalized and diagnosed with depression. He missed 140 votes. “When people hear the word ‘depression,’ many think it simply means feeling sad. But depression is so much more than that. It is physical. It is emotional,” Kean said in a closely watched floor speech upon his return. “Until you experience it yourself, it is difficult to fully understand how powerful this illness can be.” Follow live updates on the midterm elections His absence was one of the stranger episodes in recent memory in Washington. As reporters asked questions and speculation mounted, Kean’s office said he was dealing with a “personal medical issue” but declined to provide any specifics or answer questions. Reporters from NBC News and other outlets knocked on the door of Kean’s New Jersey home, but no one answered. Adding to the confusion, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and other GOP leaders said they had spoken to Kean or his family but refused to provide any explanation about why he was missing from the public eye. From the outset, Democrats believed they had a strong candidate in Bennett, a healthcare executive who, like Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, is a former Navy helicopter pilot. She attacked Kean for voting for President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which she said enacted Medicaid cuts for thousands of people in New Jersey’s 7th District, and dinged him for his votes supporting Trump’s war with Iran. As for Kean, his name is synonymous in New Jersey politics with a family lineage stretching to the American Revolution. He criticized Bennett for her ties to healthcare companies that his campaign ads said denied coverage to patients and overbilled taxpayers. “This election is common sense versus crazy; go with the commonsense guy,” Johnson said while he was campaigning with Kean in New Jersey. While he was missing from work, Kean’s office tried to make it appear he was keeping busy. His office posted almost daily on X, Instagram and other social media sites, continued to author legislation and submitted remarks to the Congressional Record that make it appear he was in the Capitol delivering speeches. “I rise today to commemorate the 65th anniversary of the Jewish Federation of West Central New Jersey,” read an entry from Kean on June 2.

articles.title: Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George elected mayor of Washington, D.C.
articles.summary: Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected mayor of Washington, D.C., NBC News projects, continuing Democratic control over the capital city — but with a twist, as self-identified socialists make gains in cities across the U.S.
articles.body: Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected mayor of Washington, D.C., NBC News projects, continuing Democratic control over the capital city — but with a twist, as self-identified socialists make gains in cities across the U.S. Lewis George will be Washington’s first new mayor since 2015, succeeding Muriel Bowser, who did not seek re-election after three terms and is leaving public office. A large number of Democrats crowded into the primary in June for the right to be the party’s shoo-in nominee in November. No Republicans ran. Lewis George, a D.C. Council member, beat Robert L. Gross of the DC Statehood Green Party and independent Rhonda Hamilton for the seat. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Lewis George’s ascension in Washington comes on the heels of other municipal successes for democratic socialists in recent years. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is the highest-profile mayor who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also identifies as a democratic socialist, though she is not a member of the DSA. Lewis George will be responsible for managing the capital’s relationship with the federal government and President Donald Trump, who posted after her Democratic primary win that he would not let Washington “be destroyed by a Communist adherent.” Lewis George said at the time: “The fact is that the mayor of our nation’s capital and the administration are going to be meeting with each other. I’m willing to work with anyone, including the administration, to improve the lives of D.C. residents, and I will stand up to anyone who puts our city or its residents in harm’s way. Making D.C. safe and more affordable for our residents is my immediate focus.” Lewis George has served on the D.C. Council since 2020, and during her campaign she championed universal childcare, expanding affordable housing and making city buses free for residents enrolled in SNAP benefits. It was the first time the city has used ranked choice voting for its mayoral race, as it was approved as a ballot measure in 2024.

articles.title: Kathy Hochul’s Win in New York Assures a Hollywood Home for Years to Come
articles.summary: The pro-entertainment governor coasted to victory. Producers (if not California officials) should feel elated.
articles.body:
Outside of California, no state matters more to the entertainment business than New York.

After all, the industry was arguably born in the region — Manhattan is where Thomas Edison held the first public screening of his Kinetoscope and Westchester County was an early hub of silent film and a movie star getaway. In the century since, New York has proven an irreplicably cinegenic backdrop. (Apologies to Sydney and Toronto, but there is simply no substitute.) It's also a second home to countless celebrities who enjoy the luxury of changing seasons.

And of course it's where so many film and television productions currently shoot — now even more than California. So what kind of leadership will Hollywood East see after Tuesday's elections? Here's the breakdown. Governor's Race — Hochul Prevails This one wasn't exactly a nail-biter, but Hollywood will surely rejoice that the Democratic incumbent, Kathy Hochul, handily fended off her Republican opponent, Nassau County executive Bruce Blakeman, leading by 47 points with about a fifth of the votes tallied. NBC News has called the race. (The silver lining for Blakeman is that the loss will overshadow his previous claim to fame as "guy whose ex-wife married Paul McCartney.")

Under Hochul's governorship, New York has made bold efforts to grow its cinematic footprint. It appears to be working : the state drew $1.6 billion in production spend last quarter, bringing it within striking distance of California as the film industry's preferred shooting location. It's no surprise that Hochul earned the endorsement of three of the area's major entertainment unions, namely Actors' Equity, IATSE and AFM Local 802.

After decades of watching states like Louisiana, Georgia or New Mexico siphon off film investment and concomitant cultural prestige, New York passed a massive tax credit program worth $800 million a year through 2036 (plus $100 million dedicated to maximizing the benefits for indie productions). Meanwhile, new soundstages have cropped up all around the five boroughs to welcome the expected influx of productions. "Governor Hochul understands that film and television production means jobs, small businesses and a thriving creative economy," Adam Gordon, who co-founded Astoria's Wildflower Studios with Robert De Niro, told THR . "She has been a real champion for this industry and we're enthusiastic about what comes next." Gordon said that Wildflower, which was completed in 2024, is now 100% occupied. Among recent productions to have filmed there is this month's Focker-in-Law .

Hochul further ingratiated herself to the industry by signing the nation's first laws regulating artificial intelligence in media and advertising . To top it off, she reversed outdated, Footloose -ian restrictions on dancing in New York bars — with the support of Kevin Bacon .

Her supporters may want to cut a rug tonight.

N.Y. Districts 13 and 37 — New Kids on the Bloc New York Mayor — and cinematic scion — Zohran Mamdani may not have been on the ballot, but the rising progressive kingmaker can take partial credit for the resounding victories of insurgent, DSA-aligned congressional candidates he championed in their primary challenges against moderate Democratic incumbents, particularly Darializa Avila Chevalier (NY-13) and Claire Valdez (NY-37). Chevalier, who rose to prominence as a leader of the Pro-Palestinian student movement at Columbia University following Hamas's October 7, 2023, attacks in Israel, has embraced unabashedly radical policies, including abolishing prisons. (Her most inflammatory past statements could be found in her Twitter history, which she deleted ahead of her primary victory in the spring.) As she heads to Washington, Chevalier is poised to supplant Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as the left's congressional lightning rod, especially since AOC seems eager to cede lightning-rod duties as she moderates some of her positions ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Chevalier and Valdez —who represents a large chunk of Queens — together with other newly enthroned representatives including Melat Kiros (CO-TK) and Adam Hamawy (NJ-TK), are set to form the core of a progressive coalition within the Democratic caucus, which some are calling "the Bloc," a younger successor to "The Squad," the AOC-led faction that came to power during the 2018 Blue Wave, halfway through Trump's first term. The two campaigned with popular streamer Hasan Piker in the all-important primary, as he both supported the candidates and took some victory laps with their wins.

NY – 17 — She Fought the Lawler (and the Lawler Conceded) The most dramatic development in the New York races today was the glitch — reportedly a programming error — that affected voting machines in northern Westchester and delayed the tabulation of ballots in one of the states most closely watched congressional contests, representing parts of four different counties.

As a result, votes from predominantly blue Westchester continued to trickle in even as NY-17's red counties had wrapped up its count, gradually shrinking two-term Republican incumbent Mike Lawler's early lead to zero, then putting Democratic challenger Cait Conley ahead. Lawler conceded the race around 11 P.M., before the race had been officially called by any major news organization. "No matter the outcome, every vote should be counted, and that is what is going to happen, and it's going to happen tonight, and we are going to make sure, one way or the other, we have an answer as to the results tonight," Mike Lawler told reporters , according to the New York Post . Quickly quashing voting-machine-related conspiracy theories might seem atypical of a party that, following the President's lead, has sought to sow doubt ahead of the election. But Lawler is among the most moderate of GOP congressmen, representing a Hudson Valley district where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans. Conley, a retired Army officer who served six tours overseas, has likewise staked out moderate positions, realizing NY-17 lies well outside the Mamdani-verse. The political newcomer has sought mainly to campaign on lowering the cost of living and to tie her opponent to Trump's unpopular tariffs and foreign wars. Among the Hollywood figures to have weighed on this race are Carrie Coon ( The Gilded Age; The White Lotus ), who campaigned for Conley , and Edie Falco (The Sopranos; Nurse Jackie ), who endorsed the Democrat — as did former Bill Clinton and Barack Obama aide (and Ari brother) Rahm Emmanuel.

articles.title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats tear up Trump's political map with historic midterms victories
articles.summary: Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds turned out to be slam-dunks for the Democrats.
articles.body:
Democrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.

With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.

Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate.

They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.

Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025.

As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.

But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.

Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.

In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.

He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.

The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory.

Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.

In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.

Adam Hamilton won Kansas' Senate seat - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.

James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.

Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.

Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also flipped a Republican Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.

Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed looked on course to beat Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.

Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans.

Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.

Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.

Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.

Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.

They are projected to win at least 239 House seats and the Republicans at least 161 seats.

A look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.

Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana.

Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.

Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.

And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.

In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans.

In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.

If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.

Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds in his bid for governor.

And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.

Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate.

He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.

On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.

articles.title: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first Black woman governor in US
articles.summary: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, won the race for governor in the southern state of Georgia on Tuesday, making her the first Black woma...
articles.body:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, won the race for governor in the southern state of Georgia on Tuesday, making her the first Black woman elected to the top office in any US state, media projections showed.

CNN and NBC News called the race in her favor.

Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate. Outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp was term-limited and could not run again.

Her win returns the governor's office to Democrats after more than two decades of Republican control.

The result is a setback for President Donald Trump, who endorsed Jackson in July and campaigned with him in the Atlanta area in the closing weeks of the race.

Former president Barack Obama rallied for Bottoms in Georgia in late October.

Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff also won re-election on Tuesday, defeating Republican congressman Mike Collins, in a result that confirms Georgia's status as a key swing state after it backed Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024.

Bottoms served as Atlanta mayor from 2018 to 2022 and did not seek a second term. She then joined the Biden White House as director of the Office of Public Engagement and later served as a senior adviser to Biden's 2024 reelection campaign.

During her campaign, Bottoms promised to expand Medicaid, lower costs for families and protect voting rights.

Jackson entered the race in February and presented himself as a political outsider who had grown up in Georgia's foster care system.

He spent more than $100 million of his own fortune on the campaign and defeated Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones, Trump's original pick, in a June primary runoff.

articles.title: Gonzalez defends battleground House seat in Texas
articles.summary: Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is projected to win reelection in Texas’s 34th District, defeating GOP challenger Eric Flores to defend the battleground sea...
articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is projected to win reelection in Texas's 34th District, defeating GOP challenger Eric Flores to defend the battleground seat, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The South Texas lawmaker was first elected to the House in 2016, serving three terms representing Texas's 15th District before winning the 2022 race for the state's 34th District.

The moderate Democrat served on the House Financial Services Committee and has introduced bipartisan legislation aimed at supporting the state's oil and gas industries and to increase transparency around military funding.

The Democrat campaigned on lowering living costs, safeguarding benefits for seniors and veterans, protecting women's rights, and expanding access to healthcare and education.

The 34th District runs along a stretch of Texas's border with Mexico and covers part of the Rio Grande Valley, including a portion of Corpus Christi and the border city of Brownsville.

The district — which was redrawn in the GOP's favor in 2025 during a mid-decade redistricting push led by state Republicans — includes a large Latino population and is considered a swing district. Just a little more than 50 percent of voters in this district supported former President Biden in the 2020 presidential election, while nearly 55 percent backed President Trump in the 2024 race.

Flores, the Republican nominee in this race and a U.S. Army veteran, put up a competitive fight after handily winning the state's GOP primary election. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rated the November race as a "toss-up."

The incumbent lawmaker's victory marks a win for House Democrats as they fight to regain their majority in the lower legislative chamber.

articles.title: Moore wins Alabama Senate race to succeed Tuberville

articles.body:
Rep. Barry Moore (R-Ala.) is projected to win the race to succeed Alabama GOP Sen. Tommy Tuberville, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Tuberville, a former college football coach, decided to exit the upper chamber after one term to run for Alabama governor.

The result is also a victory for President Trump, who backed Moore in the race to keep the Senate seat in the deep-red Cotton State in Republican hands. The president won Alabama by 30 percentage points in 2024.

In a Senate campaign announcement video , Moore touted being the first elected official in the country to endorse Trump for president in 2015, saying he "didn't wait to see which way the wind was blowing."

Moore, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, served three terms in the House and was previously in the U.S. Army National Guard. He became the Republican nominee after defeating U.S. Navy SEAL Jared Hudson in a June runoff .

Moore had been all but certain to defeat Democrat Everett Weiss, an attorney who won a runoff himself . The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rated the Alabama Senate seat as "solid Republican."

articles.title: Democrats win control of the House of Representatives with a vow to combat Trump
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Democrats will take control of the House next year, giving them the power to investigate Trump and advance legislation to check his policies.
articles.body: Democrats won control of the House of Representatives with what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades, NBC News projects, as voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republicans. The House projection is based on an analysis that Democrats will win about 255 House seats — an estimate that could still tick up or down by a few seats but will be well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority. NBC News has projected the Democrats will also flip control of the Senate, putting them in charge of both chambers. Democrats needed to win a net of just three seats to take back the majority. The blue wave washed over many more GOP-held seats than that — from the East Coast to Texas’ Rio Grande Valley — most in districts that Trump carried in 2024. A quartet of GOP incumbents in Pennsylvania were defeated. Democrat Bob Harvie beat GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a leader of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus; Democrat Bob Brooks knocked off GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th Congressional District; Paige Cognetti bested GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District; and Democrat Janelle Stelson ousted GOP Rep. Scott Perry, a former chairman of the far-right Freedom Caucus, in the 10th District. In Virginia, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria won back her old seat, defeating Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans in the Virginia Beach area, while Democrat Shannon Taylor upset longtime GOP Rep. Rob Wittman outside Richmond. Another big name in Republican politics, Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey, lost his race for re-election to Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., the first Ukrainian-born member of Congress, who frequently clashed with Trump and GOP leaders, also was defeated. And in Colorado, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel trounced GOP Rep. Gabe Evans. One of the biggest prizes of the night for Democrats was Richard Ojeda II’s upset of Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C. As chairman of the House GOP’s campaign arm, Hudson was responsible for protecting GOP incumbents and the majority. The Democrats’ victory was widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s unpopular policies, including his tough immigration crackdown, the eight-month Iran war and tariffs on U.S. allies that drove up the prices of gas, groceries and other goods. When the party takes control of the chamber on Jan. 3, it will be the first time in Trump’s second term that he won’t have full control of Congress. Since he returned to the White House, Trump has tested the limits of his executive powers, dismantling federal agencies through the Department of Government Efficiency, unilaterally imposing sweeping tariffs and rescinding congressionally approved funding — all while the GOP-controlled House and Senate mostly looked the other way. Follow live updates on the midterm elections The House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign, is expected to make history on Jan. 3 when he is sworn in as the first Black speaker of the House. He walked into his election night watch party to raucous cheers as the rap song “Unbelievable,” by the Notorious B.I.G., played on the speakers. The midterm results show the “American people are crying out for transformational change,” Jeffries told supporters. “Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land, in the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea. The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said at the gathering in Washington. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people,” he said, “and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.” With their new majority, Democrats will take control of House committees, gaining subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations of Trump’s administration, family and business ventures. That could take up considerable time and resources for Trump and his allies, forcing uncomfortable public hearings or prompting legal showdowns over subpoenas. And in a callback to Trump’s first term, some Democrats have vowed to impeach him for a third time, though there is an internal debate about whether that’s the right political path. Jeffries told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out” on impeachment. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., now poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee in January, said his panel plans to focus on “Trump family corruption,” including Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures, which have earned him more than $1 billion. The panel will also scrutinize “abuses” by ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, corporate corruption and the Jeffrey Epstein files. Aside from investigative power, House Democrats will also command the ability to pass legislation with a simple majority. Jeffries has said Democrats would focus on four areas: reversing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, extending the Affordable Care Act credits, restoring congressional authority related to tariffs and stopping Trump’s war with Iran. “I wouldn’t characterize it as investigating them like crazy. We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries told reporters at Democrats’ campaign headquarters before the election. The results are a blow to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who was launched from obscurity into the top job and has led House Republicans for the past three years. It’s unclear whether Johnson, a close Trump ally, will fight to remain as minority leader or step aside; the latter would trigger a fiercely competitive GOP race to replace him. House Democrats had the political wind at their backs; they needed to flip a net of just three seats to win back the majority they lost in 2022. And Trump’s dismal approval rating was a major factor in the GOP’s loss. Historically, the president’s party tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Only in two midterms in the modern era did a party buck that trend — in 1998, when voters punished Republicans for impeaching President Bill Clinton, and in 2002, as President George W. Bush rallied support in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Still, the battle for House control played out primarily on GOP turf this cycle, with Democrats already holding 215 seats, including a dozen in battleground districts. On top of that, results of this cycle’s mid-decade redistricting wars ended up favoring Republicans slightly, though Democrats quickly moved to neutralize what could have been a large GOP advantage. Trump fired the first shot in the summer of 2025, when he urged GOP allies in Texas to redraw their congressional lines to help the party pick up as many as five seats. Republicans also redrew maps in places like Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Missouri in a bid to win more seats. But Democrats countered in California, with Gov. Gavin Newsom, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and their allies successfully rallying support for Proposition 50, which approved a new congressional map drawn by state Democrats. That map helped Democrats pick up GOP-held seats. While the GOP successfully picked up a handful of majority-Black, Democratic-held seats in the South, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri Republicans’ new congressional map, essentially preserving the Kansas City seat of longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. “We made a promise to aggressively push back against the MAGA extremist effort to rip the election away from the American people by gerrymandering the possibility of Democrats winning the majority out of existence,” Jeffries said before the election, adding that the redistricting wars will continue in the 120th Congress. “This fight is not over; we’ve just gotten started,” he added. “It will continue into the next Congress until we pass legislation signed into law by a future president that will prohibit mid-decade gerrymandering from ever happening again.”

articles.title: Georgia governor's mansion projected to flip blue for first time in nearly 30 years
articles.summary: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as the first Black woman elected governor in America, flipping Georgia blue after over two decades.
articles.body: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is projected to win Georgia's gubernatorial race against Republican businessman Rick Jackson — flipping the governor's mansion blue for the first time in more than two decades. Fox News Decision Des projects the former Atlanta mayor will become the Peach State's first female governor and the first Black woman elected governor in American history. The victory marks a major breakthrough for Democrats in one of the nation's most closely contested swing states. Georgia voters had not elected a Democratic governor since Roy Barnes won the 1998 election and took office in 1999, with Republicans capturing the governor's mansion in 2002 and holding it ever since. GOP GOVERNOR CANDIDATE SKIPS DEBATE AGAINST FORMER BIDEN ADVISOR, REPLACED BY EMPTY PODIUM Fellow Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff also won his race for reelection, Fox News Decision Desk projects. Bottoms, who served as Atlanta's mayor from 2018 to 2022, later joined former President Joe Biden's White House as a senior advisor and director of the Office of Public Engagement. She emerged from the Democratic primary to face Jackson in the open-seat race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive and first-time candidate, poured more than $200 million of his personal fortune into his campaign. He defeated Trump-endorsed Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the Republican primary runoff , setting up the general election against Bottoms. The race drew national attention in a state that has shifted from a longtime Republican stronghold into a presidential battleground. Biden narrowly carried Georgia in 2020, becoming the first Democratic presidential candidate to win the state since Bill Clinton in 1992, before President Donald Trump returned it to the Republican column in 2024. GIANNO CALDWELL: BOTTOMS RAN ATLANTA INTO THE GROUND. WE CAN’T LET HER DO IT TO GEORGIA Bottoms campaigned on expanding Medicaid, raising the state's minimum wage and increasing pay for public employees, while Jackson called for phasing out Georgia's income tax and pitched himself as a political outsider who would bring a businessman's approach to state government. Jackson repeatedly targeted Bottoms' record as Atlanta mayor, while Bottoms attacked the Republican's massive self-funding and sought to tie him to Trump. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bottoms' victory ends a Republican run in the governor's office that began with Sonny Perdue's election in 2002 and continued through the administrations of Nathan Deal and Kemp. Fox News' Charles Creitz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrat Amy Acton wins Ohio’s race for governor
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Acton, the state’s former health director, has defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become Ohio’s first female elected governor.
articles.body: Democrat Amy Acton has won Ohio’s race for governor, defeating Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, NBC News projects. The race became hostile in its closing days after Ramaswamy’s campaign produced and aired an attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother. Acton, 60, is the first woman to be elected governor of the state. Former Lt. Gov. Nancy Hollister served as governor for 11 days in 1999 after Republican Gov. George Voinovich moved on to the Senate. She is also the first Democrat to win Ohio’s governorship since Ted Strickland won a single four-year term in 2006. Since then, the state has moved decisively to the right, and it backed Donald Trump by comfortable margins in three straight presidential elections. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Ramaswamy, 41, lost despite an endorsement from Trump and having top strategists from his and Vice President JD Vance’s political teams advising him and an aligned super PAC. “Because of your hard work, Ohio has chosen unity and decency over division and hate,” Acton told supporters in her victory speech in Columbus. “The healing begins today. We must never give up on one another. This was a tough race, but the campaign is over, and I want to make something very clear to the people of Ohio. I will be a governor for all Ohioans. I am in this fight for all of us.” Addressing his supporters in Columbus, Ramaswamy said: “It was a tough race. It was bitter at times, in both directions.” Ramaswamy added that he was hopeful that Acton could “bring Ohio together, to bring our voters and our citizens together, to lead Ohio to the best place possible.” Acton will succeed term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican whom she served under as health director during the early days of the Covid pandemic. Acton and Ramaswamy found themselves in an increasingly expensive and acrimonious fight as polls showed Democrats with a strong chance of winning the governorship for the first time in 20 years. Neither candidate has held elected office, though Ramaswamy made an unsuccessful bid against Trump for the GOP presidential nomination in 2024. Down the stretch, Acton refused to debate Ramaswamy, with her campaign manager saying she had no interest in “platforming a scam artist.” The most seismic development in their battle came two weeks before Election Day, when Ramaswamy’s campaign announced it would spend $4 million to air an ad in which Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, called her daughter a liar and urged Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton has said she has not seen or spoken with Arthur in nearly 50 years and has accused her mother’s then-husband of sexually abusing her as a child. The ad did not mention details of the abuse case, but it drew wide bipartisan condemnation from DeWine and others who saw it as exploiting a family’s painful history. Ramaswamy refused to take down or apologize for the ad. “My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his struggling campaign, but it’s not going to work,” Acton said Oct. 24 at a rally with former President Barack Obama in Cleveland. Ramaswamy, who vowed to reduce property taxes and phase out the state’s income tax, poured a considerable amount of his own money into his campaign. Meanwhile, the pro-Ramaswamy super PAC took millions of dollars in donations from fellow billionaires Elon Musk and Jeffrey Yass. Acton held up her service in a Republican administration as an example of her ability to appeal to all political sensibilities. She presented herself as a moderate in terms of tone and policies while characterizing Ramaswamy as extreme. She also spoke often of having grown up poor in Youngstown while she tried to make Ramaswamy’s wealth a liability as voters wrestled with high prices. She and her Democratic allies repeatedly criticized Ramaswamy for traveling the state in a private jet. Ramaswamy’s high-flying ways became such a focal point that even some of his fellow Republicans expressed annoyance over his insistence on the luxury. Others speculated that Ramaswamy’s Indian American heritage and Hindu faith in a state that is overwhelmingly white and Christian might hold back his campaign. Ramaswamy acknowledged the deluge of racism and bigotry he was encountering online when he announced he had deleted social media apps from his phone. Ramaswamy and his allies focused on Acton’s role as the state health director during Covid. The job made her a household name in Ohio, giving her the launchpad she would eventually use to run for governor. But it also made her a convenient villain for Republicans, who relentlessly attacked her for her involvement in closing schools and businesses — never mind that DeWine, a Republican, had the final say. DeWine has since said that attacks on Acton’s work during the pandemic are unfair. Acton, 60, also faced scrutiny over a report of a “domestic dispute” after police responded to an incident at her home in 2019. Acton, who was not charged with a crime, has described the matter as a “verbal argument” with her husband over her working hours. Ramaswamy and Republicans spent considerably on ads that sensationalized the incident and emphasized a police report that said Acton told officers she had been drinking and taken an unknown amount of prescription drugs. Acton’s campaign has said that she was not intoxicated and that the medication was something she had taken regularly for years. Trump traveled to Ohio to lend his support to Ramaswamy in person. He noted, though, that Ramaswamy ran against him briefly in 2024. “He was not easy,” Trump said at an Oct. 3 rally in Vandalia, near Dayton. “This one was not easy. He was a nasty guy. But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He’s actually got a great heart.”

articles.title: Former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra wins California governor’s race
articles.summary: Becerra, a longtime fixture in Democratic politics in the state, beat Republican Steve Hilton, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Democrat Xavier Becerra has been elected governor of California, NBC News projects, defeating Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton, who was considered an underdog. Becerra, 68, was elected to a four-year term to succeed Democrat Gavin Newsom, who is term-limited and could run for president in 2028. California, the largest state in the country, hasn’t elected a Republican governor since Arnold Schwarzenegger in 2006. Donald Trump lost the state by 20 percentage points in the 2024 election. Becerra was health and human services secretary in the Biden administration. Before that, he was California’s attorney general, a member of the House for 12 terms and a member of the state Legislature for two years. In Congress, Becerra held leadership roles, including chairing the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and the House Democratic Caucus. Becerra ran on a platform of battling the Trump administration and painted Hilton as a candidate who would rubber-stamp Trump’s policies. Follow live updates on the midterm elections “As Governor of California, I vow to protect and lead our state against Trump and his attacks. When Trump and his administration threaten access to healthcare, affordable housing, fair wages, or protections for immigrants and marginalized communities, the state has a responsibility to step in and fight,” Becerra’s campaign website said. “I am that fighter, and have a proven record facing and winning against Donald Trump, having sued him 122 times in fact as California’s Attorney General.” Becerra’s platform also called for lowering healthcare costs, building more homes to address the state’s housing crisis, addressing price gouging and rate hikes, embracing “clean energy” and calling for investments in disaster mitigation as the state has been devastated by wildfire, floods and earthquakes in recent years. Becerra also advocated for a policy of regulating AI but also promoting its benefits in government and schools. He argued that data centers can “add value” to the state’s energy infrastructure but that they must meet environmental disclosure requirements. Becerra faced criticism from alumni of the Biden administration over his leadership managing multiple health crises at the Department of Health and Human Services. They denounced his handling, for example, of the Covid pandemic, a baby formula shortage, an outbreak of the mpox virus and the arrival of a large number of unaccompanied children at the U.S.-Mexico border. But he advanced to the general election in June from a crowded all-party primary field after former Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell dropped out of the race in April amid sexual assault and misconduct allegations, which he denied. Hilton, a former Fox News host, had also advanced to the general election in June over billionaire Democrat Tom Steyer and Republican Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco. Hilton, originally from the United Kingdom, became a U.S. citizen in 2021. Trump had endorsed him in the governor’s race in April. Becerra touted his experience taking on the Trump administration as the state attorney general and pointed to his experience in the federal government as reasons to elect him. Hilton attacked his tenure in the roles, saying his work didn’t help resolve the state’s problems. During CNN’s gubernatorial debate in September, Becerra lambasted Hilton’s tax plans. “What I wouldn’t do, Steve, is try to convince the people of California that proposing Trump tax policies, promising Trump tax cuts, believing you’re going to get better results than Trump has gotten so far to date, that that is what — isn’t it the definition of insanity you do the same thing over and over again expecting different results?” he said.

Steve Hilton during a California gubernatorial debate in February. Laure Andrillon / AP

articles.title: Democrat David Crowley wins the Wisconsin governor’s race
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, defeated GOP Rep. Tom Tiffany, maintaining Democratic control of the office in the swing state.
articles.body: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley has won Wisconsin’s race for governor, NBC News projects, defeating Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany and keeping the office in the critical swing state under Democratic control. Crowley is the first Black person to be elected governor of Wisconsin. At age 40, he’s also the youngest governor to be elected in the state in nearly a century. He succeeds two-term Gov. Tony Evers, who helped resuscitate his primary campaign this summer. Crowley managed to overcome the massive campaign cash advantage held by Tiffany, who represents a largely rural area in the northern part of the state in Congress. He highlighted an affordability agenda that proposed cutting costs of household expenses like childcare, healthcare and housing, mostly through a proposed increase in state spending. Crowley also put his personal story front and center for voters. He grew up in one of the poorest areas of Milwaukee, and his family struggled with poverty and homelessness when he was a child, while both of his parents dealt with drug addiction. Before he was elected Milwaukee County executive in 2020, Crowley served in the state Assembly and worked as a community organizer and political aide. Tiffany struggled to overcome the political headwinds his party faced nationally. In the lead-up to Election Day, polls showed voters in the state holding increasingly negative views of President Donald Trump, and Crowley used many of his campaign ads to cast Tiffany as a loyal Trump acolyte. Tiffany and his GOP allies attacked Crowley for raising property and sales taxes as Milwaukee County executive and over statements he had made in support of undocumented immigrants. His fundraising edge was driven almost entirely by the support of three billionaire megadonors. Down the homestretch of the campaign, Crowley received support from several high-profile national Democrats, including former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore. Crowley’s win caps a surprising turnaround for his campaign. He had suspended his primary campaign in July as he polled in the low single digits, only to relaunch it just 10 days later alongside a big endorsement from Evers. Heading into the primary, polls showed state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, with a clear lead. But moderate Democrats who feared Hong was too far to the left to win a general election in Wisconsin rallied behind Crowley at the last minute, leading to his victory by fewer than 4,000 votes. Some Democrats feared Crowley’s unexpected primary victory gave him a relatively short runway to introduce and define himself to voters across the state. Tiffany, by contrast, did not face a competitive primary after having secured Trump’s endorsement. And as the Republican ad barrage took hold, polls showed a stark increase in the percentage of voters who viewed Crowley unfavorably. But Crowley’s base in Milwaukee County, along with support from Dane County — the state’s two most populated and most heavily Democratic areas — gave him a critical boost.

articles.title: Xavier Becerra wins California governor race
articles.summary: The expected win gives California its first Latino governor.
articles.body:
SACRAMENTO, California — Xavier Becerra will succeed Gavin Newsom as the next governor of California after emerging from a chaotic primary and then cruising past Republican rival Steve Hilton, according to The Associated Press.

The former Biden health secretary will immediately confront a thorny set of problems that include an affordability crisis, long-term budget deficits, deep federal health care cuts, and a hostile Trump administration that has repeatedly targeted California.

At a moment when populist fervor is sweeping the country, Becerra won as an establishment Democrat, presenting himself to voters as a steady leader who could address some of California's most pressing problems — above all the state's soaring cost of living — while defending it against President Donald Trump. He largely eschewed grandiose policy promises and touted a record that includes stints as a member of Congress, state attorney general, and President Joe Biden's Cabinet.

While his victory over Hilton was all but inevitable in deeply Democratic California, it marked a historic moment as a son of Mexican immigrants became the first Latino governor in California's modern history.

A growing Latino electorate has transformed California politics over the course of Becerra's lifetime, helping to turn the state into a Democratic stronghold and giving rise to a generation of Latino political figures — including Sen. Alex Padilla and both Democratic leaders in the state Legislature.

Despite his long history in public service, Becerra is viewed by much of the California political establishment as something of a mystery. He ascended only after better-known Democratic contenders passed on running or, in the case of former Rep. Eric Swalwell, dropped out amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied.

He has shared few concrete details about his agenda, but has offered some clues. He has pledged to take on wildfire liability after Newsom failed to push a deal through this year and said he would ensure Californians retain their health insurance in the face of federal cutbacks.

articles.title: Talarico Wins Texas Senate Race, First Democrat to Win Statewide in More than 30 Years
articles.summary: Talarico is the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas since 1994.
articles.body:
James Talarico just accomplished what no other Democrat in Texas has done in three decades: winning a statewide race.

Talarico cruised to victory against Ken Paxton, with the Associated Press calling the race late Tuesday. The outcome ends what had become one of the longest winning streaks in U.S. politics. Talarico is the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas since 1994 . He is also the first Democrat to be elected Senator by Texans since 1988.

Most polling heading into Election Day showed Talarico, a state legislator and seminarian, running ahead of Paxton, the scandal-plagued state Attorney General who has faced criminal inquiries and narrowly dodged an impeachment conviction by his fellow Republicans in Austin. Both in Texas and around the country, interest in the race was sky high. More than 7.7 million votes were cast ahead of Election Day

For many Texas Democrats, Talarico's win is vindication in a longheld belief that demographics in that state were destiny. Democrats have argued for years that Texas wasn't as Republican as election results suggested, but rather a state with so many non-voters that a Democrat could win with the right candidate and message. This cycle proved them correct, as early vote numbers matched the numbers during 2024's presidential election and ran well ahead of the 5.1 million who voted early in 2022.

But Talarico certainly played a central piece in this history-making moment. A plain-spoken former Teach For America alumnus, his message was a blend of progressive optimism and faith-tinged evangelizing. Talarico worked to build an unlikely coalition that included plenty of folks who had been reliably Republican votes in the recent past. As clips of his speeches and interviews went viral he quickly became a political star with a national following, one who also became one of the cycle's best fundraisers.

Both Paxton and Talarico fought for their party's nominations in expensive primaries. The price tag for just ads in the race approached three-quarters-of-a-billion dollars. Outside spending brought $534 million in advertising, with Paxton enjoying a roughly 2-to-1 advantage. The bulk of that came courtesy of Elon Musk, the world's richest person and a Texas resident. The ally of Trump flooded the state with $224 million of support for Paxton. The eye-popping outlay proved for naught.

Republicans never quite figured out how to campaign against Talarico. Trump gave him the nickname "Talafreako"—which Talarico's campaign embraced and turned into campaign merch. The persistent rumor that he was a vegan in meat-loving Texas ricocheted in the MAGAverse but photos of Talarico eating barbecue quickly dispelled that. In the race's final days, no less than Vice President J.D. Vance offered a crude joke that Talarico is gay. (He is not.)

While Talarico sought to expand Democrats' tent, Paxton seemed to focus almost entirely on turning out his base with the help of Trump, who broke with party leaders in Texas and Washington and endorsed Paxton over incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn.

Republican strategists insisted that Cornyn would be in a far stronger position to hold the seat, particularly among fears of a blue-wave midterms. There were also concerns that Paxton would have trouble fundraising enough to match Talarico.

As one GOP strategist bemoaned, every dollar spent holding the seat in Texas was a dollar that was not being used to flip seats in Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, or Georgia. Some estimates pegged a GOP rescue mission at $250 million . Even that whopping figure under-estimated the ultimate cost in a state bigger than most countries in size and population.

Trump at first refused to endorse either Cornyn or Paxton in the race. Once the primary went to a May runoff, he formally backed Paxton, all but ending Cornyn's political career. So worried were Republicans about holding the Texas seat that they scheduled the highly unusual midterm political convention in the state to try to gas their base.

Even after endorsing Paxton, Trump's support for the nominee was uneven. In speeches, he would waver between championing Paxton and making digs at his likeability and appearance.

Paxton struggled with a clear message in the race. His tenure as the state's Attorney General—once seen as a strength among a base that loved his fights against Democratic Administrations—became a liability as his accumulation of wealth during his years in public office drew allegations of cronyism. And he refused to debate Talarico, who pushed for such an event, even offering to let Fox News moderate it.
