articles.title: Democrat ousts De La Cruz in key Texas House race, flipping battleground seat
articles.summary: Democrat and Tejano music star Bobby Pulido will defeat Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the race for Texas’s 15th Congressional District, Decision Desk...
articles.body:
Democrat and Tejano music star Bobby Pulido will defeat Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the race for Texas's 15th Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ projects, a big win for Democrats in a key House battleground.

Polling ahead of the race consistently showed Pulido in the lead despite the district's Republican lean , with a Texas Southern University poll in mid-October showing Pulido ahead 51 percent to De La Cruz's 44 percent.

Pulido entered the race already well known by voters in the area — but not for his political experience. The Texas Democrat has a storied career as a Tejano music star with multiple Latin Grammy awards.

In a 2023 interview with The Hill, Pulido teased an entrance into politics ahead of his performance at the Congressional Hispanic Caucus Institute's Awards Gala.

He drew national attention for his viral moments, frequently performing at his own rallies, and even offering to perform at quinceañeras and other events for families across the district. After a storied career as a musician, Pulido will now head to Congress.

He ousted De La Cruz, a two-term incumbent. De La Cruz was the first Republican to ever represent the 15th District since its creation, as Democrats have historically dominated politics in Texas's Rio Grande Valley.

But South Texas shifted dramatically toward Republicans in recent years. While Democrats used to win the 15th easily, it swung hard to the GOP throughout the decade, with President Trump ultimately carrying it by nearly 20 points in 2024.

Pulido's victory marks a rebound for Democrats among Latino voters in a district where they make up nearly 80 percent of residents.

Texas was ground zero for the mid-decade redistricting war of the midterm cycle. Republicans redrew five Democratic-held seats hoping to protect their House majority in 2026, three of them in South Texas. While the 15th was not one of the redrawn districts, Pulido's race was one of Democrats' few chances to strike back at attempted GOP gains.

Pulido will be sworn in on Jan. 3 along with the new Congress.

articles.title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa takes down Texas Gov. Greg Abbott in stunning result
articles.summary: Hinojosa, a state representative, will be Texas’ first Democratic governor in more than three decades and its first Hispanic governor, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa has defeated Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a three-term Republican, NBC News projects, wresting control of the red-state governorship from Republicans for the first time since 1995. Hinojosa’s projected victory, which will make her the state’s first Hispanic governor, comes after Abbott’s campaign outspent her by tens of millions of dollars. Abbott, who could have become Texas’ longest-serving governor had he won, initially looked poised to earn another term in what has been a ruby-red state for decades. But changing demographics and a steadily worsening political environment for Republicans across the country and in Texas, where GOP nominees for several offices faced personal scandals and criticism, eventually took their toll on Abbott, too. In a victory speech, Hinojosa said Abbott called to congratulate her and promised big changes coming to Texas. “I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state,” Hinojosa said. “The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get.” Follow live updates on the midterm elections Hinojosa, who was born and raised in the Rio Grande Valley, was elected to the state House in 2016. Before she became a legislator, she was a civil rights and a labor lawyer. Education has been a pillar of her political career, with Hinojosa crediting work to stop her son’s elementary school from closing because of state budget cuts as her inspiration to seek elected office. Education funding and reform were big issues in her campaign, as she pledged over the summer that one of her first actions as governor would be to fire the state’s education commissioner, citing declining student performances across Texas. She also criticized Abbott on data centers, a big issue throughout the state, including in rural areas. While Abbott has enjoyed reliable support from rural voters in past races, he faced friction with the voting bloc this cycle over his past support of data centers. Texas is home to over 500 data centers thus far, making it the state with the second-most data centers in the country. Abbott has walked back some of his support for developing data centers; he ordered the state to stop approving data center permits in September, while an audit was conducted of data centers’ effect on Texas’ electrical grid. Hinojosa charged in ads that Abbott was “doing the bidding of his billionaire donors” and that he was “selling out Texas” by supporting data center construction. Hinojosa, who is a fluent Spanish speaker, also connected with Latino voters, who make up around one-third of the state’s electorate, throughout the campaign, both by releasing bilingual TV ads and holding town hall meetings in Spanish. Abbott, meanwhile, hammered Hinojosa for being “radical.” He used campaign ads to target her past support for transgender female athletes and gender-affirming care for minors, calling her “Gender Bender Gina.” “They want to run an entire campaign saying that I’m too woke. I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke,” she replied in an ad. “That’s the difference. I’m Gina Hinojosa. My pronouns are mom, Texan and soon-to-be governor.” Voters never saw a single debate between Hinojosa and Abbott. Hinojosa criticized Abbott for not responding to debate invitations, eventually staging a debate outside the Governor’s Mansion in mid-October.

articles.title: Democrat Sherrod Brown unseats Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, completing comeback bid
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Brown, who lost a re-election bid in 2024, will return to the Senate after he defeated Husted, a Republican who was appointed to succeed JD Vance.
articles.body: Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown has prevailed in one of the year’s most combative and expensive Senate races, beating Republican incumbent Jon Husted, NBC News projects. Brown, who lost his bid for a fourth term in 2024, will return to the Senate and serve the remaining two years of the six-year term JD Vance won in 2022 and left after he was elected vice president. Republican Gov. Mike DeWine apointed Husted, the state’s former lieutenant governor, to fill the Vance vacancy last year. The win cements Brown, 73, as the most successful Democrat in Ohio over the last three decades. For Husted, 59, defeat presents an uncertain future for a long-tenured officeholder. The race brought an onslaught of negative TV ads. Their clash also mirrored a national climate that exposed Republican vulnerabilities on issues such as the war with Iran, a related rise in gas prices and broader concerns about the economy and affordability. And worries over data center construction for AI companies hit particularly hard in Ohio. In the race’s closing weeks, an ad in Ohio’s other marquee race — the battle for governor — raised concerns that backlash against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy could hurt Husted. Ramaswamy’s campaign had put $4 million behind an attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. Acton has not seen her mother since her then-stepfather was charged with raping her as a child nearly 50 years ago. As a tech-focused lieutenant governor, Husted championed data centers as a way of the future — a position that Brown and Democrats relentlessly exploited over the course of the campaign. The issue loomed as such a liability for Husted that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in an August memo that it could doom his candidacy. Husted, whose early endorsement from President Donald Trump helped him avoid a messy primary, also overcame concerns that he was running a halfhearted campaign. It was no secret that the Senate was not his first choice. He had been running for governor, a position he has long coveted, when the Vance vacancy shook up Ohio politics. Husted faced a potentially grueling Republican primary for governor against Ramaswamy, a friend and businessman who also was preparing to launch a campaign for the job. Instead, Husted accepted DeWine’s appointment to Vance’s seat while keeping his $6 million gubernatorial war chest intact — a Plan B, in the eyes of some GOP observers. “I’m, like, an Ohio guy. D.C. is not my place,” Husted said at a Stark County GOP picnic in August. “When my flight goes in on Monday, I’m a lot less happy than when I’m coming home on Thursday, right? But I understand how important it is. You have to have somebody there that knows your state, is going to fight for you.” Brown faced persistent scrutiny over his 50 years in public office. Husted and Republicans framed him as a career politician with little to show for it. In addition to the data center attacks, Brown tried to characterize Husted as an unflinching Trump loyalist who supported the Iran war and initially voted against the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files. Over the final weeks of the race, Trump mounted a vigorous defense to keep Husted in the seat, rallying with him in the state twice in nine days. Both rallies included cameos from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who played football with Husted at the University of Dayton. Trump marveled about Husted’s physical form and athleticism, which he said he was unaware of until he learned about it from Gruden. “I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete,” Trump said at an Oct. 12 rally in Youngstown. “And I looked, and I watched up and down, and I looked at his ass, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. ... He’s got these, like, claws, and I got it. You are a great athlete. I didn’t know that, because he doesn’t talk about that. Congratulations! Now they finally know.”

articles.title: Democrat Matt Little wins Minnesota House race to succeed Craig
articles.summary: Democrat Matt Little is projected to win Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Little defeated Republican state Sen....
articles.body:
Democrat Matt Little is projected to win Minnesota's 2nd Congressional District , according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Little defeated Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt in the race to replace retiring Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.). Craig opted to run for Senate but ultimately lost the Democratic primary to Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

The Democrat led his opponent 59.8 percent to 40.2 percent with 69 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11:05 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Little's win comes in a district that has steadily shifted left in recent elections, despite Republican efforts to make inroads with suburban voters in the North Star State.

The former state senator and Lakeville mayor ran on a progressive campaign, calling for "Medicare for All," changes to federal immigration enforcement and a moratorium on new data centers .

He also took aim at President Trump's handling of the Iran war, arguing the U.S. should withdraw from the conflict.

DDHQ's preelection forecast showed Little with a 96 percent chance of winning, compared with Pratt's 4 percent.

The Republican, a four-term state senator, sought to portray himself as an independent voice who could work across party lines. He emphasized lowering healthcare costs, cutting government waste and leaving decisions about data center development to local officials.

The two former legislative colleagues sparred during an October debate over health, Trump's foreign policy moves and their records in the Minnesota Legislature.

articles.title: Trump's gamble on Ken Paxton backfires as Democrat pulls off historic Texas Senate upset
articles.summary: James Talarico flipped Texas' Senate seat for Democrats after Trump's backing of Ken Paxton backfired amid corruption allegations and a GOP schism.
articles.body: Democrats just made history in Texas. President Donald Trump’s gamble on Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a strong ally of the president’s, backfired on him after Texas state Rep. James Talarico pulled off an upset to score Democrats their first Senate seat from the Lone Star State in nearly four decades. The Fox News Decision Desk called the Texas Senate race in Talarico's favor shortly after 11 p.m. ET Tuesday night. The live music rarely stopped Tuesday at Talarico’s election night party, except for when it was confirmed that the insurgent Democrat had toppled Paxton. News of his victory replaced the thundering music with an eruption of cheers, chants of USA and a wave of joy that reverberated through the event space. Even Talarico’s most staunch, four-legged supporter, Kodak, was roused from a nap. His owner told Fox News Digital that the canine fan had voted for Talarico earlier that day. TRUMP BACKS PAXTON IN TEXAS REPUBLICAN SENATE SHOWDOWN WITH CORNYN It comes after Trump opted to back Paxton over longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, earlier this year, who Republicans in Washington, D.C., believed would be a better candidate during a midterm cycle in which political headwinds, spurred by economic stress and war, pushed back against the party in power. Cornyn posted on X when Talarico won, "The voters have spoken, and I want to extend my congratulations to James Talarico on his election to the U.S. Senate. I look forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate." Trump made near-weekly visits to the Lone Star State, and his deep-pocketed war chest, MAGA Inc., along with national Republicans, dumped hundreds of millions of dollars to support Paxton’s struggling campaign. But it was not enough to overcome the insurgent Talarico, who styled himself a moderate dedicated to representing Texans and not Democratic interests, like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s, D-N.Y., in Washington. It was a bitter campaign from start to finish, with Talarico painting Paxton as unfit to serve following several allegations of corruption, including his impeachment for alleged corruption by the Texas House. He was later acquitted by the Texas Senate. REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES "This Senate seat has been held by some of the finest Texans," Talarico said. "Ken Paxton should be nowhere near Lyndon Johnson's Senate seat. Ken Paxton should be nowhere near Sam Houston's Senate seat." Paxton, Trump and national Republicans painted Talarico as a "communist" and a vegan in BBQ-loving Texas and zeroed in on his support for the transgender community while in the Texas Legislature, most notably his floor speech on God being "nonbinary." "I'm not asking you to imagine what I do as your U.S. senator," Paxton told voters at a rally ahead of Election Day. "I'm asking you to look at my record and then compare it to another guy, James Talarico, the most radical Democrat ever to run statewide, bar none. "And no matter how many commercials he runs lying about his record, James Talarico is a, simply put, a Democratic Socialist just like AOC. And just like the New York mayor, Mamdani." JAMES TALARICO BLAMES RISE IN GOP 'EXTREMISM' FOR PROMPTING HIS 'GOD IS NONBINARY,' SIX SEXES REMARKS Talarico even scored a nickname from Trump. "The name happens to be ‘Talafreako’ because he is one of the worst candidates I have ever seen," Trump said ahead of the GOP’s midterm convention largely meant to bolster Paxton’s struggling campaign. Nonetheless, there was a schism within the GOP caused by Trump picking Paxton over Cornyn, and the longtime lawmaker made it clear that he would not be in Paxton’s corner campaigning for him after losing a bloody and bitter primary fight earlier this year. "Judgment Day is coming for Ken Paxton." The news comes on a brutal midterm election night for Republicans at both the state and federal levels. articles.title: Missouri voters block Republican-drawn congressional map
articles.summary: Missouri voters blocked a GOP-drawn congressional map from going into effect for future elections via a ballot measure, NBC News projects.
articles.body: Missouri voters blocked a GOP-drawn congressional map from going into effect for future elections via a ballot measure, NBC News projects. The result is a blow for Republicans, who fought for more than a year to carve up one of the state’s two-Democratic-held districts. The vote was the culmination of a long-running political and legal fight. Missouri is one of the GOP-led states that heeded President Donald Trump’s mid-decade redistricting call, passing new lines last year that drew longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver into a heavily Republican district. In response, a group called People Not Politicians Missouri said it gathered more than 300,000 signatures — well above the 106,000 necessary — to place a referendum on the ballot that gave voters the opportunity to veto the map. Legislation facing such a referendum is typically put on hold until voters have weighed in, but Missouri Republicans fought to put the map in place for this year’s midterms. State Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, waited until the statutory deadline in August to announce that he wouldn’t certify the referendum for the November ballot, saying it was unconstitutional. The issue ricocheted through the state and federal court systems, at times producing conflicting rulings. Ultimately, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected Missouri Republicans’ attempts to use the redrawn map for this year’s elections three times. Nine states enacted new congressional maps ahead of the 2026 midterms, outside the traditional process that occurs every 10 years after the new census. The mid-decade redistricting battle is expected to extend into the next election cycle, with Democratic-led states continuing to try to counteract Trump’s initial push and Republican-led states responding to a major Supreme Court ruling this year that opened the door to dismantling majority-Black districts represented by Democrats.

articles.title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa elected Texas' first Latina governor, ousts Republican incumbent Greg Abbott
articles.summary: AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abb...
articles.body:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott and catapulting a decided underdog to the helm of what has long been the nation's most populous red state.

She will become Texas' first Latina governor — and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards in the 1990s — following a groundbreaking victory that topples one of the nation's most prominent Republican governors and steadfast supporters of President Donald Trump, possibly accelerating the state's shift to an emerging battleground.

Her victory was part of an electrifying night for Democrats in Texas, where James Talarico also won election , defeating Republican Ken Paxton in the race for the U.S. Senate.

Hinojosa's win served as validation for Democrats' long deferred dream that demographic changes in the state would be followed by a shift in political power. It also elevates Hinojosa, a 52-year-old state legislator from a liberal Austin district since 2017, into a breakout Democratic star, even as she did not have significant support from the national party for her campaign.

"It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us," Hinojosa told supporters at her victory party in Austin. "Texas, my faith in you never wavered."

Jumping in the race with little money or name recognition, Hinojosa engineered a plucky and populist challenge, railing against artificial intelligence data centers and corruption to down Abbott. She also proved that money in politics has clear limits. Billionaire Elon Musk had spent tens of millions of dollars to back Republicans, and Abbott's campaign had spent $180 million since last year in what was thought to be a safe path to a fourth term.

But Hinojosa proved durable while simultaneously riding the tailwinds of Talarico's hard-charging Senate campaign , one of the nation's marquee races. Just two years after Trump carried the state by double digits, the upset is also a stark reflection of how a glum national mood dragged down Republicans even in a stronghold where Democrats had not won in decades.

Trump blamed Abbott for the loss in a striking criticism of one of his staunchest supporters, accusing him of becoming a "RINO," or Republican in name only, in the last months of the race. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn't pretty!" Trump posted on social media.

Abbott, who had been seeking a record fourth term, said he called Hinojosa and pledged to help her transition into office.

"Leading this state has been the greatest honor I've ever had," Abbott told supporters as he conceded the race.

On a national level, the loss will set off alarms for Republicans, who depend on winning Texas in presidential election years to maintain a path to the White House.

The first Democrat elected governor since 1990

How Hinojosa governs is likely to open a dramatic political and cultural shift in the Texas Capitol, which over the last decade has passed one of the nation's strictest abortion laws and increasingly aggressive immigration crackdowns .

Abbott, who first took office in 2015, won each of his previous races by double digits.

Then came Hinojosa, who started her campaign last year at a time when bigger-name Democrats seemed uneager to wade into the race.

From the start she accused Abbott of prioritizing the wealthy over everyday people and failing to bring down costs. Abbott said Hinojosa wanted to raise taxes and painted her as a radical and a threat to Texans' way of life.

One of Hinojosa's earliest campaign pledges was a one-time $1,500 payment to each of the state's nearly 32 million residents that she called a "Corruption Tax Refund." She said the money would come from Texas' massive emergency savings fund.

Hinojosa also seized on growing national rejection of data centers, accusing Abbott of allowing the energy-guzzling server warehouses to multiply. Abbott responded to public anger with a temporary moratorium on new data center approvals.

Hinojosa distanced herself from the progressive label

Hinojosa was once a proud vice chair of the Texas Legislative Progressive Caucus and defender of transgender rights, which became a centerpiece of Abbott's attacks.

She tried to shake off the progressive label throughout the campaign and batted away culture-war issues, presenting herself instead as a populist. Her campaign included ads featuring Republican voters saying they would support her.

At her victory party, Hinojosa told the crowd that "your life can be bigger than your dreams" in a speech that described her upbringing on the Texas-Mexico border and outlined her policy priorities, including fighting for public schools.

"Texas will bow down to no one," she said.

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Elon Musk's last name.

articles.title: Andrews defeats Graham, becomes first Democrat to win U.S. Senate seat in SC since 1998
articles.summary: Dr. Annie Andrews will be the next U.S. Senator for South Carolina.
articles.body:
Dr. Annie Andrews will be the next U.S. Senator for South Carolina.

ABC declared Andrews the winner over Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

She becomes the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Palmetto State in nearly 20 years.

The race took an unexpected turn after the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham. His sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to temporarily fill his seat before seeking a full term.

Andrews, who had been campaigning for more than a year, reshaped her strategy to face a new opponent.

"And I know that the work ahead won't be easy," said Andrews Tuesday night. "But after 18 months and 4 counties and everything we've been through together, I've never been more certain of one thing: South Carolina's best days are still ahead of us."

Sen. Graham took the stage Tuesday night to thank her team and supporters for their work this election season, but that wasn't enough.

Graham said she called Andrews and congratulated her on her win. She also thanked President Trump, who personally asked Graham to run for this seat.

President Trump campaigned twice in South Carolina last month asking voters to support Graham, but ultimately his base did not back Graham as much as it backed Trump in key places in 2024.

Graham said it is clear the party has work to do.

"Tonight was not what we expected," Graham said. "It is clear that we as conservations have work to do and that work starts tonight."

This loss means that for the first time in more than two decades, a Graham will no longer be in the Senate.

Sen. Darline Graham is hoping to win the seat held by her brother Lindsey Graham for more than two decades.

Typically, this would be easy to do in a solid red state. But Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews has provided some competition.

Darline Graham was appointed to fill the rest of her brother's term when he passed away earlier this year.

Then President Donald Trump encouraged her to run for the full term, something she says she wanted to do to make her home state safer and stronger.

Annie Andrews, a Charleston-area pediatrician, filed to run before Lindsey Graham's death.

She spent years working in children's hospitals, and says what she saw families facing through her work in healthcare pushed her into politics.

Both have affordability as one of their top priorities.

"I'm all for a balanced budget amendment. I want to cut spending. I want to cut taxes. I want to bring jobs manufacturing back to this country," Darline Graham said. "I want to lower taxes on the middle class. I'm the only one in this race that has released a taxpayer pledge to address the $40 trillion debt to lower taxes on the middle class to cut out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government."

This race seems to be closer than a lot of people anticipated a few months ago.

There have been a lot of twists turns, the biggest being the unexpected death of the original Republican nominee Sen. Lindsey Graham, and his sister replacing him on the ballot.

In Charleston, the goal of the Andrews campaign has always been to unseat the Republican and become the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Palmetto State since 1998.

Her campaign focused on being a moderate voice that isn't scared to break with her party in Washington for the betterment of the state.

She spoke to Channel 9 about that on Tuesday, and why she believes Graham would do the opposite.

"I was not recruited to run by my party," she said. "My party isn't funding me or writing my scripts. Unlike my opponent, who was very publicly handpicked by her party bosses to be in this seat and to be the nominee for this race."

Sen. Darline Graham on the other hand ran for this seat after she was appointed to finish her brother's tern in the Senate.

She says her goal is to continue his legacy. She says her record of working in state government for decades shows that she won't shy away from working for South Carolina.

"I've been working for the people of South Carolina for thirty years," she said. So, it was a way for me to continue serving. I use the word serve because that's the way I see it."

Regardless of what happens, history will be made in South Carolina Tuesday night.

Either candidate will be the first female U.S. Senator in South Carolina to be elected to the seat.

articles.title: Josh Turek flips Iowa Senate seat, giving Democrats a boost in the fight for the majority
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Turek, a state lawmaker, has defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in a state that has trended red in recent years.
articles.body: Democrat Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to take Iowa’s open Senate seat, NBC News projects, a critical flip for his party in the fight for the majority. Turek, a state representative who won a contested primary this year with the tacit backing of Democratic leaders in Washington, effectively tied Hinson to President Donald Trump and a Republican agenda in Washington that proved unpopular with voters in Iowa. Turek hammered Hinson on her repeated votes backing Trump’s trade war, which has hurt Iowa producers and consumers, and the war with Iran, which has contributed to rising prices for gas, diesel fuel and products that are transported into and around the state. The victory could not have come at a more opportune moment for Democrats. To wrest control of the Senate from Republicans, they needed a net gain of at least four seats. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Iowa in nearly two decades. Hinson leaned heavily on her record over three terms in the House and Iowa’s Republican tilt, but she could not overcome Trump’s sagging approval ratings and voter frustrations about the cost of living. As was the case across the country, Trump and his agenda played an outsize role in the Iowa race. Hinson was forced to perform a high-wire act in which she simultaneously courted Trump’s MAGA base and tried to find ways to distance herself from him. In September, after the last of her seven votes against efforts to end the war, Hinson announced that she believed the conflict should come to an end. That positioned her closer to the sentiments of Iowans but gave Turek the opening he needed to call her a flip-flopper. On Oct. 21, the day Trump held a rally in Sioux City to bolster Hinson and other Republican candidates in Iowa, Hinson told “NBC Nightly News” anchor Tom Llamas that she was not disappointed in Trump. But despite a voting record in lockstep with his priorities, she argued that she has no trouble working with — or standing up to — presidents of both parties. “I work alongside the president. When he’s right for Iowa, I’m going to tell him. When he’s wrong for Iowa, I’m going to tell him,” she said. “But that’s not a change for me in how I’ve operated. I’ve always worked with both sides to get things done for Iowa.” Hours before Trump’s arrival, she separated from her party’s leaders by condemning Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring the mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton. In the ad, which Trump and Vice President JD Vance expressed support for, Acton’s mother accuses her of being a liar. Acton and her brother say they were removed from the family home after allegations that her mother’s husband sexually abused Acton. “It’s terrible. I think about it as a mom, and you think about your kids surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again,” she told ABC News. “I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down.” Democrats’ bet on Turek’s narrative, and his ability to prosecute the case against Trump and Hinson, paid off. Born with spina bifida, which he attributes to his father’s exposure to Agent Orange in Vietnam, Turek won gold medals in wheelchair basketball at the Summer Paralympics in 2016 and 2020. He then won election to the Iowa state House in 2022, becoming the first permanently disabled member of the Legislature. He faced a divisive primary against state Sen. Zach Wahls in June but ended up cruising to victory, 63% to 37%. Hinson had an easier path to her party’s nomination because Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott of South Carolina endorsed her in the fall of 2025, helping her clear the field of serious opponents. She won her primary with 75% of the vote in June. Turek appeared to be the preferred candidate of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — though neither officially endorsed him — and Wahls used the signs of their support to paint Turek as beholden to them. Hinson picked up on that argument and also accused Turek of standing with the far left of his party. She hammered him for missing votes in the Legislature in the early part of the year as he campaigned for his party’s nomination. In debates and on the campaign trail, she noted that President Joe Biden signed two of her bills into law — one on preventing stillbirths and one to create a federal study of rural veterans’ mental health. Rather than pick fights with Trump, Hinson found niche ways to distance herself from the national party. As one of the marquee matchups on the map, Iowa’s race attracted about $200 million between the two candidates’ committees and outside groups — more than the $167 million annual appropriation for state agriculture and natural resources programs Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds signed into law this summer. The money kept flowing in large part because the race looked so close. For months, surveys showed a contest within the margin of error, with some finding Hinson in the lead and others finding Turek ahead. In the end, Hinson was unable to free herself from the Trump anchor that Turek tied her to.

articles.title: Democrats capture full control of Congress, NBC News projects, fueled by victories in deeply Republican states
articles.summary: Democrats capitalized on voter anger over Trump and affordability, flipping seats in deep-red and major battleground states alike.
articles.body: President Donald Trump told voters to pretend he was on the ballot in this year’s midterm elections. They did. And they resoundingly rejected both his policies and his Republican Party. Democrats have captured full control of Congress, NBC News projects, with voters delivering a forceful repudiation of Trump’s agenda, coupled with a clear-cut message that Congress has not done enough to provide checks on his administration and needs to do more to address affordability and corruption. Democrats’ victory in the Senate comes after a swift and decisive win in the House, where Democrats are set to have what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades. Democrats flipped six Republican-held seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Some of those states Democrats had long dreamed of turning blue, and others were barely even on their radar a year ago as possibilities. In a number of those states, Trump handpicked the nominees, sometimes over the objections of members of his own party who were concerned that they would be weak in the general election. An early warning sign that it would be a tough night for Republicans came when South Carolina — a state even many Democrats thought was out of reach — fell early. Democrats made incursions deep into the heart of MAGA country, with gains far beyond what they were able to achieve in the 2018 midterm elections during Trump’s first term. Forty-three percent of midterm voters surveyed in the NBC News Exit Poll said one of the reasons they voted the way they did was to express opposition to Trump, whose job approval rating is lower than that of any president on Election Day in nearly two decades. Seventy-one percent of voters — including 41% of Republicans — also said there is not enough congressional oversight of Trump. Corruption, affordability, immigration and the war in Iran were all key issues, as well. The results were so bleak that Trump quickly ran away from them Tuesday evening. Trump said on social media that, in fact, he was not on the ballot, and that’s why Republicans lost: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The Democratic takeover will reverberate widely. With majorities in both chambers, the Trump administration will now have to contend with checks and investigations it avoided with a compliant Congress in Republican hands. The election results could influence the makeup of the Supreme Court, the arc of the 2028 presidential race and the fate of Trump’s legislative plans in the back half of his term. But it also sets up an epic showdown with Trump that will test the constitutional power-sharing arrangement that has weathered war and civil strife over the past two centuries — but survived intact. With their newly minted majority, Democratic lawmakers will acquire an arsenal of oversight powers they’ll use to investigate a Trump administration they contend has escaped accountability. Trump, in turn, has built a presidency rooted in a vision of unrivaled executive power. Neither side seems in a mood to compromise, meaning the next two years could bring legislative and executive branch clashes unlike anything since the Watergate era. “What we’re going to do is lower costs, end all this rampant corruption and end the chaos. Plain and simple,” Chuck Schumer of New York, the Senate’s Democratic leader, said before the election in response to a question from NBC News about his priorities if his party won. Democrats’ sweeping victory looked inconceivable when the midterm campaign season kicked off. The party prevailed despite an unfavorable map in which the major battlegrounds ran through red states that Trump won in all three of his presidential bids. Not since 2006 has the minority party flipped control of both chambers on a single night. Then-President George W. Bush, facing a voter backlash over the Iraq War, memorably lamented that the outcome was “a thumping.” Trump sought to mobilize his core voters and preserve the GOP’s narrow majority in the House and the Senate by putting himself front and center. He kept up a packed campaign schedule in the final month of the campaign, but he and his party were dogged by his low job approval ratings, along with pronounced voter frustration with the economy. Trump sought to blame his predecessor, Joe Biden, for rising prices, but voters didn’t seem to buy the argument. Gas prices spiked after Trump and Israeli leaders launched the Iran war in late February, and Americans disliked Trump’s handling of the conflict, creating another drag on Republican candidacies. The election results are apt to make history, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on the cusp of becoming the country’s first Black House speaker. Democrats are expected to hold their internal leadership elections the week of Nov. 16, when Jeffries will become his party’s nominee for speaker. Then, on Jan. 3, he must win 218 votes — a simple majority of all House members — to formally win the speaker’s gavel and become second in the line of presidential succession. Schumer, who previously served four years as Senate majority leader, is expected to return to the top job once again after he exceeded expectations and led his party back from exile. Democrats had been favored to win the House all season; they needed to flip a net of just three GOP-held seats to do so, and historically, the president’s party loses dozens of seats on average during midterm elections. But as the campaign unfolded, Democrats grew more bullish about winning the Senate, as well. One reason was the minority vote. Latino voters helped propel Trump’s political comeback in 2024, but they turned away from him this cycle, citing high prices and his immigration crackdown. An NBC News poll released Sunday showed that Democrats enjoyed a 27-point lead among Latino voters, a marked contrast from the election in 2024, when Trump lost by only 7 points in the demographic. The outcome could also leave an imprint on the Supreme Court. Before the election, multiple Senate Democrats cast doubt on whether they would confirm any Trump nominee to a vacancy on the Supreme Court if one were to arise in his final two years. With full control of the Senate, Democrats are positioned to block nominees Trump puts forward. “Well, given the history of Trump nominees, I think it is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Judiciary Committee, told NBC News in an interview before the elections. “Because we’ve seen this movie, we know how it ends, which is a politician in robes who is following Trump’s orders on most major questions.” Looking ahead, the election results could recast the fight for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. The presumed GOP front-runner is Vice President JD Vance. But if the outcome amounts to a rejection of Trump and his brand of politics, Vance may find that he has no glide path to the nomination. As the minority party, Democrats lacked the power to issue subpoenas and schedule oversight hearings. That all changes come January, when the new Congress convenes. Democratic lawmakers are already signaling that they will look to rein in the spending and war-making powers Trump has wielded with little pushback from a compliant Republican-led Congress. House Democrats have vowed to carry out aggressive oversight of Trump’s family, business dealings and administration, including the ICE and Homeland Security immigration crackdown and Trump’s pet renovation projects at the White House and other Washington-area landmarks. At the tip of the spear of the investigations are Reps. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee. Garcia has outlined his investigation strategy, focusing on what he calls “Trump family corruption,” including how Trump’s fortune has grown by billions of dollars since his 2024 campaign, as well as Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes and Trump’s immigration crackdown. Judiciary Committee Democrats said they also have a long list of investigative targets that includes pardons for “wealthy criminals and MAGA loyalists,” and foreign governments’ “buying influence” through gifts and payments to the Trump family’s crypto empire. Jeffries has said that Democrats aren’t focused on impeaching Trump but that they also haven’t ruled it out. Trump was impeached twice during his first term but acquitted both times by the Senate. “The cost of living is way too high, and Donald Trump — along with his Republican sycophantic members of Congress — have actually decided not to do anything about it because so many of them are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends and their donors. There is a cost to corruption,” Jeffries told reporters before the election. “These are all things that are going to need to be thoroughly investigated as part of our pledge to hold the crooks accountable, beginning on day one,” he said. Given the election results, Republicans may be motivated to usher in pieces of their legislative agenda during the lame-duck session before they officially relinquish control of the House on Jan. 3. They could include another party-line “reconciliation” bill to advance Trump’s spending and tax priorities, along with a debt ceiling increase before a 2027 deadline. The political future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is unknown. He would need a majority of the Senate GOP caucus in a closed-ballot election to carry on as minority leader. But he has had an up-and-down relationship with Trump, who has vented frustration with him for failing to eliminate the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act, which would overhaul the country’s election laws. Another mystery is the fate of Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who has run the House for the past three years. He could stay on as minority leader, but in the face of the defeat across the board, some rank-and-file Republicans are likely to demand new leadership.

articles.title: Evans behind in U.S. House race; Democratic Socialist elected in another race
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - Democrats appeared to be on their way to gain a U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) - Democrats appeared to be on their way to gain a U.S. House seat in Colorado Tuesday with U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Fort Lupton, far behind the Democratic challenger.

The first-term Republican congressman received 85,654 votes - 40% of the ballots in the 8th Congressional District race. Democrat Manny Rutinel, a first-generation immigrant who was born in Los Angeles, had 118,757 votes, a total of 56% in the 8th Congressional District. That's as of 9 p.m. Mountain time.

In other election news, Melat Kiros, a Democratic socialist who made headlines by defeating U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Denver, in the Democratic primary, won Colorado's 1st Congressional District seat. According to media reports, Kiros, 29, is the first Generation Z member elected to Congress.

Kiros, who supports Medicare for all, received 150,372 votes or 78% of the vote. Republican opponent Christy Peterson, an ally of President Donald Trump, had 26,689 votes, totaling 14%, with most of the counties reporting as of 9 p.m. Mountain time.

Kiros' race attracted Democratic donors from across the country, raising over $1 million since announcing her bid in June 2025, with 90% of her donations coming from individual donors. Peterson raised less than $10,000.

Evans, meanwhile, fell behind in his race despite campaign contributions from red states across the country. Individuals donated almost $700,000 in Texas and roughly $450,000 in Tennessee.

The Republican senator's campaign attracted donations totalling $7.2 million, with nearly one half coming from individual donors.

Rutinel raised roughly $9.4 million, $2.2 million more than his opponent, with almost 90% of his contributions coming from individual donations and nearly $750,000 from contributors in California.

Evans grew up in Aurora, Colo., and currently resides on a farm in Fort Lupton with his wife Anne Evans and their two kids. He served in the U.S. Army and the Colorado National Guard for 12 years and later served in law enforcement for a decade. After being elected to serve in the state legislature in 2022 for Colorado's 48th Congressional District, which covers Adams and Weld counties, Evans went on to win the general election in 2024 by less than 1% and served in Colorado's 8th Congressional district in the nation's capital beginning in 2025.

Rutinel, who was raised by a single mother who immigrated from The Dominican Republic, wrote on his campaign website that he came from a working-class family who faced financial difficulty during the 2008 recession and promised to fight for the working-class if elected.

He was endorsed by the nation's second-largest teachers union, the American Federation of Teachers; United Auto Workers and other Democratic-leaning PACs.

The winner of the 1st Congressional District race, Kiros, was born in Ethiopia and grew up in Denver. She got her law degree from Notre Dame in 2022 and worked as an attorney for a global law firm in New York City, but was fired in 2023 following a letter she published criticizing top law firms' response to the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Her political platform declared that universal childcare and eldercare is a "universal right," according to her campaign website . She has been endorsed by the independent and self-proclaimed socialist senator from Vermont, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders; Democratic Socialists of America and Justice Democrats, which has donated over $500,000 to her race.

The pro-Palestinian PAC, American Priorities, also donated $150,000 to Kiros' campaign back in June.

Peterson is a designer and accountant from Denver. She has aligned herself with President Donald Trump on numerous issues, including the need for stricter immigration enforcement and border control. The candidate also calls herself a conservative, writing in a campaign biography that "I'm running for Congress to stand up against the progressive left and communist socialism."

Peterson was endorsed by Colorado Hispanic Republicans and the National Women's Prayer and Voting Army.

Colorado's 4th Congressional District race was too close to call as of 8:30 p.m. Mountain time. U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Windsor, had 41,529 votes – a total of 47%. Democratic challenge Eileen Laubacher, a 32-year retired veteran and Navy admiral, had 150,604 votes, amounting to 50%.

Boebert went uncontested in the primary and received over 92,000 votes compared to her opponent's 72,483 votes. She has raised only about $130,000 since she filed her candidacy in April of 2026, and has received no contributions from the Republican Party.

Laubacher has accrued more than $13 million in contributions for her congressional campaign, raising nearly $2.6 million in the most recent quarter. Most of her donations came from more than 200,000 individual donors across the country.

The long-time veteran frames herself as a moderate Democrat, who proclaimed on the debate stage in mid-October that certain positions endorsed by more progressive members of her party, such as Medicare for all and open borders, were not feasible.

In Congress, Boebert remains on the House's Committee on Natural Resources, serving as the vice chair on the subcommittee on oversight and investigations. She's also on the subcommittee on water, wildlife and fisheries.

U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse, a Democrat who acted as impeachment manager for the second impeachment against President Donald Trump, won the 2nd Congressional District race with 75.38% of the ballots or 196,714 votes. Republican Kelley Anne Dennison got 23.12% of the ballots or 60,344 votes.

The 3rd District race was too close to call with Dwayne L. Romero, the Democrat, at 49% of the ballots or 125,164 votes, and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, the Republican incumbent, at 47.63% of the vote or 120,579 ballots.

In the 5th District, Democrat Jessica Killin was leading with 52% of the ballots or 118,290 votes. U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank the Republican incumbent, had 45% of the ballots or 103,246 votes.

In the 6th District, U.S. Rep. Jason Crow, the Democratic incumbent, won with 66% of the ballots or 139,325 votes. Jason Clark, the Republican, had 33% of the ballots or 66,476 votes.

U.S. Rep. Brittany Pettersen, the Democratic incumbent, won reelection to the 7th District with 62% of the ballots or 186, votes. Republican Tim Bennett had 35% of the ballots or 103,012 votes.

articles.title: Democrat seize House control in stunning blue tsunami, vow retribution against Trump admin
articles.summary: Democrats seized the House majority as an unprecedented blue wave flipped battleground districts and safe red seats in a blow to Donald Trump.
articles.body: Democrats have seized the House majority and will control the lower chamber of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term, the Fox News Decision Desk projects. An unprecedented blue wave saw Democrats pull off stunning upsets in both battleground House districts and areas considered safe red seats. The Fox News Decision Desk projects the GOP suffered major losses in four key groups: Hispanic voters, young voters, independents and rural Americans. THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS IS JUST THE BEGINNING. HERE'S WHAT'S AT STAKE ON ELECTION DAY Top Democrats did not hesitate in signaling they would be raring to go after various investigations targeting Trump and his administration. "Lawyer up," Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely next House Oversight Committee chairman, said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital. The X account belonging to Democrats on the House Homeland Security Committee posted at Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin, "Clear your calendar." Among Democrats' most stunning upset victories in the House came against Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., who switched parties from Democrat to Republican during the first Trump administration. Democrat Jamie Ager defeated his Republican challenger in North Carolina's 11th congressional district, a previous GOP stronghold that became vulnerable after retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., announced he would not seek re-election amid sexual harassment allegations. And vulnerable Republicans who have weathered tough re-election bids in the past appeared poised to fall to Democratic challengers as of shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., conceded his race to Democrat former Biden administration official Cait Conley, according to a video posted by journalist Timmy Facciola. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is now easily poised to become the country's first Black Speaker of the House, likely with a double-digit majority that will leave room for any far-left defectors. "This is a change election, and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change. Things are broken. We need a Congress that puts the American people first. The wealthy, the well-off, and the well-connected tried to buy this election. The American people have responded in a resounding way and made clear that America is not for sale. We will deliver. A Congress that puts everyday Americans first, working class Americans first, middle class Americans first, and all those who aspire to be part of the middle class," Jeffries told people at an election night party in Washington, D.C. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, multiple House Republicans told Fox News Digital that they expect new senior leaders after their existing top echelons failed to deliver. Among the names that some are floating is House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, who has been campaigning for GOP candidates in the months before Election Day. House Republicans are holding their internal leadership elections next week.

articles.title: Key moments so far in the US midterms
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.
articles.body:
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Even before results are finalised, the night has provided some historic results and scenes of celebration. These are some of the key moments so far.

Democrats talk of 'great American comeback' after historic results

Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Republican President Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.

Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.

"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.

If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Jeffries.

Trump congratulates opposition on 'good job'

Trump has spoken throughout the night to a number of media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".

He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Texas.

Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."

Cheers as Democrats win first Senate flip of the night in North Carolina

There were cheers from supporters in North Carolina as the Democrats secured the night's first flip of a Senate seat.

The state's former Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, won against Republican candidate Michael Whatley.

"Tonight we show the country that when everyday people come together, we can make change," Cooper said as he addressed his supporters on Tuesday.

The last time the Democrats won a Senate race in the state was 2008, despite the party making enormous investment in time and money behind their candidates in recent contests.

Democrats win control of US House and take first Texas Senate seat in decades

Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Republican territory with historic wins

Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first black female governor

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, has been projected to win the governor's race in Georgia, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.

The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue, which came after the state's former senator said the party was "nauseously optimistic" about their chances this year.

Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive, who was endorsed by outgoing Governor Brian Kemp and President Trump, who spent $200 million of his own money on the race.

The state has also not had a Democratic governor in more than 20 years.

Ossoff victory in Georgia adds fuel to 2028 speculation

As well as Bottoms being elected the new governor of Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has been projected as the winner of the Senate race there , giving him a second term.

His victory was not unexpected as he had a comfortable lead in the polls over his Republican challenger Mike Collins - a member of the lower House chamber.

Ossoff told his supporters following his victory that for those who "doubted whether our republic would survive" over the last two years, the "first light of dawn is on the horizon".

Republicans had hoped this would be a more competitive race because the Peach State has been reliably Republican for decades. Trump also won it in the 2024 presidential election, after Joe Biden eked out a narrow victory there in 2020.

Now that he has won re-election in the Senate, the speculation surrounding Ossoff's plans for the next presidential election in 2028 will likely increase - he is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring.

Chris Pappas celebrates with husband as first openly gay man elected to Senate

Democrat Chris Pappas has also made history as the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.

Pappas is projected to defeat former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race - who comes from one of the state's political dynasties having seen his father and brother serve as governor.

But the contest between the two was well-natured, with Pappas thanking his opponent on Tuesday by saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."

The 46-year-old Pappas had represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 but chose not to run for re-election so he could launch his campaign for the Senate.

articles.summary: See the maps and charts that show how America voted in the US midterm elections.
articles.body:
It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats so far in the US midterms.

They have taken control of the Senate and are projected to take control of the House of Representatives too, according to the BBC's partner CBS News.

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.

Texas , Iowa , Ohio and Maine have also turned blue. There is one toss-up seat to come in Alaska and even Mississippi is now on a knife edge, according to CBS News.

Polls before the election saw South Carolina as leaning Republican. It had been a deep red seat for many years, last returning a Democratic senator in 1998.

The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday). The Democrats are making the gains they need to take control but have their sights set on a much bigger victory.

Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.

The redistricting saw both districts move from having a majority of 2024 Kamala Harris voters to having a majority of people who voted for Donald Trump.

Florida 22, which was also redrawn to favour the Republicans, saw a victory for the Democrats too.

Hispanic voters turn to Democrats in Florida

Hispanic voters look to be one of the key groups in the elections in Florida. A huge poll of voters suggests that this group backed the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon by 55% to 44% for the Republican Angie Moody.

This is a turnaround from the estimated 55% of Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024.

The poll also asked what issues voters were most concerned about. It suggests that across the country the economy was the biggest issue, followed by the state of democracy.

When voters were asked if Donald Trump's policies impacted economic conditions, the poll suggests more that two-thirds believe they had made things worse.

articles.title: Democrat Annie Andrews wins US Senate seat in South Carolina upset
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrat Annie Andrews won a US Senate seat in conservative South Carolina on Tuesday, according to media projections, ousting...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrat Annie Andrews won a US Senate seat in conservative South Carolina on Tuesday, according to media projections, ousting Republican Darline Graham in a state President Donald Trump carried by 18 percentage points just two ‌years ago.

Andrews, a pediatrician, is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in South Carolina in 28 years, a striking ‌gain for a party that needed a net four seats to overturn Republicans' 53-47 majority.

Andrews' win in a state that neither Democrats nor Republicans considered competitive until recent weeks embodies ​the broader rejection of Trump and his handling of the economy during the first two years of his term.

The South Carolina Senate race attracted national attention after Darline Graham's brother, US Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly in July. Trump lobbied Governor Henry McMaster to appoint his sister — a little-known state employee who had never held elected office — to fill the late senator's seat and publicly encouraged her to run for the full term.

She defeated US Representative ‌Ralph Norman for the Republican nomination in an August ⁠runoff, but divisions lingered. Norman told local media that he would vote for her but his family would not, and he declined to campaign with her.

Graham's inexperience was on display during a Republican runoff debate in August, when ⁠she said she was not "that informed on national security" and that national security was "not my thing." Senate Majority Leader John Thune did not endorse Graham but said she was a strong candidate. Former Republican Governor David Beasley and former Democratic Governor Jim Hodges jointly endorsed Andrews.

Republicans had privately worried that Graham was a ​weak ​candidate, according to a party strategist who spoke on condition of anonymity, and grew ​increasingly frustrated when the national party had to divert ‌resources to prop her up. Republican outside groups poured $27 million into holding the seat, while Democratic groups invested $24 million to flip it.

Graham has said she was "not a polished politician" but defended her candidacy, saying during an October debate against Andrews that she was "just as qualified" as her opponent.

Trump's approval rating has held near a career low amid voter discontent with the Iran war, high diesel prices and the cost of living, putting once solidly Republican seats into play.

Trump held a rally in the state last week as the race tightened, where Graham told supporters ‌her opponent was "batshit crazy." In response, Andrews asked Graham if it was crazy "to want ​cheaper gas and groceries."

Democrats notched surprise wins in other closely watched House and Senate ​races in their drive to retake control of both chambers of ​Congress. The party has vowed to launch aggressive investigations of Trump officials and cabinet members, as well as companies ‌that made concessions to the White House or capitulated to ​Trump's demands.

In addition to South Carolina, ​Democrats picked up Senate seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Texas, according to media projections.

"This night is turning into a very clear repudiation of Trump, MAGA and the Republican party," said Simon Rosenberg, a Democratic strategist.

Republicans held onto Florida's Senate seat in a ​tighter-than-expected race, as Republican Ashley Moody edged past Democrat ‌Angie Nixon.

Democrats also defended several House seats in redrawn districts meant to favor Republicans in North Carolina, Florida and other states, ​and were on track to win House seats in what had been considered safe Republican districts in deeply conservative states.

(Reporting ​by Yasmeen Abutaleb; Editing by Andy Sullivan, Howard Goller and Edmund Klamann)

articles.title: Trump's stinging midterm rebuke casts a new political landscape
articles.summary: After a decade of defining American politics, Trump's coalition shows signs of fraying with blue victories in red precincts.
articles.body:
In a stinging midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump , Democrats were poised to win control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. After a decade of defining American politics, Trump now begins a new political chapter , his trademark coalition showing signs of fraying while his opponents gain a foothold to confront him during his final two years in office.

Republicans faced losses even in red states and districts that Trump had carried by double digits just two years ago. That's the definition of a political tsunami, when the opposition's wave is overwhelming enough to swamp even distant shores.

Three of four voters said in a survey sponsored by NBC and other news organizations that they were dissatisfied or angry with the way things are going in the United States − including almost every Democrat and nearly half of Republicans. Seven of 10 voters complained that Congress hadn't done enough to check the powers of the presidency.

Midterm hopefuls vote and greet supporters

For the past two years, the weapons of Trump's Democratic opposition have been largely limited to lawsuits and rhetorical shadowboxing. After the results of Nov. 3, they will be able to wield legislative powers to investigate his administration and challenge policies on everything from safety-net spending and global tariffs to waging war with Iran.

"I have the ultimate power – it's called 'veto,'" Trump told CBS News as votes were being counted. He predicted Democrats eventually would be forced to cooperate with him. "Historically, you veto for a couple of months and then they come and say, 'We've got to make a deal.'"

"America is back," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become the first Black speaker of the House, told exuberant Democrats at an election night rally in Washington. "Today begins the great American comeback."

Democrats, who needed a net gain of three seats to control the House, were rolling well past that to a solid majority. In Senate races, where they needed a net gain of four seats to win control, their road to the majority ran through some very red states.

Democrat Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held seat in North Carolina. In Texas, which Trump carried by 14 points in 2024, Democrat James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton. And in South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews ousted Sen. Darline Graham.

Trump, who carried the state by 18 points two years ago, had hand-picked her as the nominee.

Once again, it was the economy, stupid – the mantra coined by Bill Clinton's presidential campaign more than three decades ago and one that politicians have ignored at their peril.

Nearly 9 in 10 voters in exit polls said the cost of living had been a crucial or major factor in determining their vote, and almost 8 in 10 said inflation had caused a hardship for their families. The president was getting much of the blame: By more than 2-1, 65%-28%, they said he had made economic conditions worse, not better.

Trump found himself being hammered for the issue that helped propel his election two years ago. Then, he lambasted the Biden administration for failing to control inflation. Now, voters said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans to handle the economy.

Voters leave stickers at Renee Good, Alex Pretti memorials

Then, Trump blasted then-president Joe Biden for allowing a massive influx of undocumented immigrants across what he called "open borders." Now, nearly 6 in 10 voters said Trump's immigration enforcement measures had gone too far.

In Minneapolis, voters left "I Voted" stickers at street memorials for Alex Pretti and Renee Good, who were fatally shot by immigration officers this year.

Concern about immigration was costing Republicans among some Hispanics. That voter group, like young people, had swung toward Trump in the presidential election two years ago only to fall away in the midterms Tuesday.

That said, Democrats can't count on automatically reclaiming their political loyalty. Neither party is held in high regard: Republicans had a favorable-unfavorable rating of 41%-58%. The Democratic Party fared only slightly better, at 46%-54%.

The mean streets of midterms for presidents

To be sure, midterm elections are typically tough on presidents.

In four of the last five midterms, the president's party lost control of the House. In two of them, it lost control of the Senate. Midway through Trump's first term, in 2018, Republicans lost the House though they gained two seats in the Senate.

Still, unlike his predecessors, Trump sought to make the election a referendum about him , urging voters in a final sprint of 29 rallies to "pretend" that he was on the ballot. The effort to generate turnout among his MAGA base also spurred turnout among his Democratic opposition.

That made the results unusually personal: 41% said one reason for their House vote was to express their opposition to Trump. Just 16% said it was to express their support.

With the 2026 midterms over, the 2028 presidential race begins in earnest.

Among the White House hopefuls, three Democrats sailed to easy reelection in gubernatorial contests − Wes Moore in Maryland, JB Pritzker in Illinois and Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania. Sen. Jon Osoff's reelection in Georgia fueled interest in him as a potential presidential contender.

And in Detroit, at the election night party for Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg was on stage, ginning up the crowd. He's a hopeful, too.

articles.title: Missouri voters reject ballot measure that would have banned abortion in the state
articles.summary: Voters turned down a measure, NBC News projects, that sought to ban abortion with limited exceptions and would have prohibited gender transition surgery for minors.
articles.body: Missouri voters rejected a ballot measure to ban abortion in the state constitution, NBC News projects, preserving abortion access in the state. The ballot measure aimed to impose a new prohibition that would have banned abortion in all cases except “medical emergency, fetal anomaly, rape, or incest.” In the case of rape or incest, an abortion would have been allowed only up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. Missouri narrowly voted to make abortion a state constitutional right in 2024. Before then, it had been the first state to enforce an abortion ban after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. A “trigger law” took effect immediately after the ruling, banning abortion with no exception for rape or incest. However, abortion now remains legal in the state after the new ballot measure was rejected. In addition to the abortion ban, the measure included language prohibiting gender-affirming surgery on children under 18. It would have also more permanently prohibited hormone therapy and puberty-blocking drugs from being prescribed for the purpose of gender-affirming care for minors. A state law then-Gov. Mike Parson signed in 2023 already imposes the same policies.

articles.title: Adam Hamilton wins Kansas Senate race in another Democratic upset
articles.summary: Democratic Reverend Adam Hamilton defeated GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in the Kansas Senate race, CBS News projects, unseating the incumbent in a major upset.
articles.body:
Washington — Democratic Reverend Adam Hamilton defeated GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in the Kansas Senate race, CBS News projects, unseating the incumbent in a major upset that comes as the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century.

Hamilton, 62, leads the U.S.' largest United Methodist church and is a well-known author and speaker. He took on Marshall, who was seeking a second term in the Senate after representing Kansas in the House since 2017.

Marshall, 66, is a medical doctor who worked for 25 years as an obstetrician-gynecologist and served in the U.S. Army Reserves before coming to Capitol Hill, where he's been a reliable supporter of the president's agenda. But he was put on the defensive as he sought another term in the chamber, as the race in Kansas became surprisingly competitive amid the challenge from Hamilton, a centrist Democrat.

Hamilton is a fifth-generation Kansan who ran on an affordability-focused agenda, while aiming to bring together a cross-party coalition in what at first seemed like a long-shot bid to take on Marshall. Kansas last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1932, and President Trump won the state by more than 16 points in 2024.

In Hamilton, Democrats saw a chance at flipping the seat in ruby-red Kansas as the president's unpopular war with Iran continued, causing skyrocketing diesel and gas prices. And with healthcare costs also a key issue, Marshall was in the hot seat over a New York Times investigation that found that the doctor had filed lawsuits against more than 700 of his patients over outstanding bills.

In the final weeks of the campaign, Marshall tried to distance himself from the president, criticizing the administration's immigration enforcement, for instance. National Republicans also tried to rescue Marshall, redirecting millions of dollars to defend the seat.

The development marked a major loss for Republicans, helping to seal Democrats' majority in the Senate.

articles.title: Polls close in Alaska as ranked-choice vote counting begins in key U.S. Senate race
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Polls are now closed across Alaska and the time-consuming process of determining the winner is under way. Alaska allows four candidates...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Polls are now closed across Alaska and the time-consuming process of determining the winner is under way.

Alaska allows four candidates to advance to the general election, and voters are asked to rank each of the candidates through its ranked choice voting process.

The race between incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, Democratic candidate Mary Peltola two others has been embroiled in controversy over allegations the Peltola campaign planted a spoiler candidate in the race with Sullivan's name. Dan J. Sullivan, a school teacher, and Gerald Heikes also are on the ballot.

The U.S. Department of Justice and the state of Alaska are investigating the allegations against the Peltola campaign, with the DOJ sending letters on Tuesday to people suspected of recruiting the second Sullivan to confuse voters at the polls.

As for the ranked choice voting process, if none of the four candidates are the choice of a majority of voters after the first round of counting, the candidate with the least top votes is thrown out and counting is continued using those voters' second choice. The process continues until one candidate is the top selection of a majority.

Aside from the ballot controversy, Sullivan and Peltola disagree on key issues of taxation and federal benefits for Alaskans. Peltola pushed for abolishing income taxes on Alaskans making less than $92,000 per year and expanding the child tax credit.

Sen. Sullivan has supported legislation that would inform families of tax credit opportunities but did not endorse an expansion of the credit.

Peltola held the support of 47.0% of voters over Sen. Sullivan's 44.8%, according to an average of four most recent polls compiled by 270toWin. The polls also projected spoiler candidate Daniel J. Sullivan would earn 3.5% of the vote in an average of four polls.
