articles.title: Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan holds a Minnesota Senate seat for Democrats
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Flanagan defeated Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, in a race Republicans had hoped to put in play.
articles.body: Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan defeated Republican Michele Tafoya in the Minnesota Senate race, NBC News projects, keeping the seat in Democrats’ column. Flanagan will become the first Native American woman to be elected to the Senate. Democrat Mary Peltola, who’s running for the Senate in Alaska, is also Native American. The result is also a victory for the progressive wing of the party. Flanagan, who defeated a more moderate opponent to win the nomination this summer, supports “Medicare for All,” national paid family and medical leave and dismantling ICE. While Minnesota has leaned blue in recent cycles, Republicans eyed the seat as a potential target in the wake of fraud scandals that roiled the state. In one fraud case, people are alleged to have stolen $250 million from a Covid-related program that was supposed to go toward providing children with meals. The Justice Department announced criminal charges this year against more than a dozen people in Minnesota, accusing them of defrauding Medicaid and other social services of more than $90 million. The administration sought to tie fraud cases to immigration, leading to enforcement actions, protests and high-profile violence. The former leader of the nonprofit at the center of the $250 million fraud case is white, and prosecutors have said most of the defendants are of Somali descent. President Donald Trump seized on the fact and repeatedly denigrated immigrants from Somalia. In an interview The Minnesota Star Tribune published last month, Flanagan said that any fraud was “completely unacceptable” and that “more should have been done sooner.” Asked in the interview whether she bore responsibility, she said Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, “is the one who took the lead on fraud.” Late last year, federal immigration agents launched operations in Minneapolis, and early this year, immigration enforcement shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The killings sparked widespread condemnation from critics, who pointed to the shootings as evidence of an out-of-control and unaccountable enforcement agency. Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, was a first-time candidate who framed herself as a political outsider. She supported deporting immigrants who are convicted of fraud and said she would push for new mandatory minimum sentences for fraud crimes. The seat is open after Sen. Tina Smith, a Democrat, announced last year that she would not seek another term. Republicans have long sought to put Minnesota in play. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried the state by only 4 percentage points in the 2024 election, while Sen. Amy Klobuchar cruised to re-election by 16 points.

articles.title: Sherrod Brown wins Ohio Senate race, flipping seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Sherrod Brown faced off against Husted, who was appointed to the seat last year to replace Vice President JD Vance.
articles.body:
Washington — Former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown will be returning to the Senate, defeating Sen. Jon Husted, CBS News projects. Brown flipped the seat for Democrats two years after he lost his reelection bid in the Buckeye State.

Brown, 73, lost narrowly in 2024 to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno after more than three decades representing Ohio in the House and Senate. Democrats saw a path to victory in the state this year, since President Trump's popularity has been waning because of the Iran war and high fuel and cost-of-living prices. Brown fell short by just four points two years ago, and Mr. Trump won Ohio by more than 10 points.

Brown faced off against Husted, who was appointed to the seat last year to replace Vice President JD Vance. Husted, 59, previously served as Ohio's lieutenant governor and secretary of state. He was defending the seat for the first time this cycle, and remained a relative unknown in the race.

While Brown maintained a strong working-class brand in the state, Republicans attempted to use Brown's long history in Washington to frame him as the incumbent in the race. But Brown railed against Husted on AI data centers and energy costs, in what became a defining issue in the race, framing him as "the face of data centers."

The projected victory comes as no senator since 1988 has made a successful comeback bid to the upper chamber after losing reelection, and marks a major flip for Democrats as they seek to win control of the Senate.

And while Republicans were confident about their chances heading into the midterms, competitive races opened up in several states that Mr. Trump won by double digits in 2024. Among those states the president won handily last cycle, Ohio represented the easiest pickup for Democrats, with smaller margins than Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

articles.title: James Talarico wins Texas Senate race, flipping seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico will defeat Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, CBS News projects, marking a major flip for Democrats that they have long...
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico will defeat Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, CBS News projects, marking a major flip for Democrats that they have long sought in the Lone Star State.

Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who identifies himself as a progressive Christian and ran on fighting corruption and lowering costs. He faced off against Paxton, the state's attorney general, in a closely watched Senate contest as Democrats saw their first real opportunity for a Senate victory in Texas for the first time since 1988.

Paxton, 63, defeated Sen. John Cornyn in a runoff for the GOP nomination, ousting the incumbent senator who has represented Texas since 2002 with the support of a last-minute endorsement from President Trump. After the primary, Democrats saw their chances improve, thanks to Paxton's history of personal controversies and his more conservative positions, as many Republicans lamented that they would have to spend millions to keep the seat in Texas. By mid-October, spending in the race had already topped half a billion dollars , making it the most expensive in the state's history.

The Texas attorney general was impeached by the state House in 2023 on accusations of bribery, obstruction of justice and abuse of the public trust. He was later acquitted by the state Senate. During the campaign, amid messy divorce proceedings, additional reporting emerged, including that he spent New Year's Eve in 2024 at a Dubai party with two U.S. fugitives and a woman who was not his wife. The Paxton campaign decried the reporting, without denying it, while saying he had been politically persecuted.

Paxton, and the GOP more broadly, took aim at Talarico, painting him as too extreme for Texas while pointing to previous comments he made on issues like veganism and gender, some of which Talarico has said " missed the mark " and even called "cringey" later. When Talarico was away from the campaign trail for more than a week last month with what he described as a bad case of the flu, Republicans scrutinized his whereabouts, spurring conspiracies. But the attention appeared to fizzle after Talarico's campaign shared security camera footage that appeared to show Talarico at his home in Texas during his absence from the trail.

Talarico's projected victory brought Democrats another flip, helping to cement their majority .

articles.title: Democrats flip four governorships, extending their inroads into red states
articles.summary: Democratic candidates flipped control of governorships in four races while maintaining power in several other states, further punctuating the party’s success in Tuesday’s elections.
articles.body: Democratic candidates flipped control of governorships in four races while maintaining power in several other states, further punctuating the party’s success in Tuesday’s elections. Seizing on a broadly toxic political climate for Republicans, Democrats notched victories in perennial battleground and deep red states across the map. Democratic candidates wrested control of governor’s mansions in Georgia, Iowa, Texas and Ohio. The most shocking flip came in Texas — a state Donald Trump won two years ago by nearly 14 points, where the last Democratic governor was elected more than three decades ago. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, overcoming a massive spending deficit to become the state’s first Latina chief executive. Democrats also made history in Georgia, where former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, flipping control of the battleground state office for the first time in 24 years. Bottoms’ victory means she will become the first Black female governor in U.S. history. Bottoms is one of three Black gubernatorial candidates who won Tuesday, along with Democratic Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland and Republican Byron Donalds in Florida. There has never been more than one Black governor serving at a time before. In Iowa, State Auditor Rob Sand beat Republican Zach Lahn, making him the first Democrat to be elected to lead the state in two decades. Trump won Iowa in 2024 by 13 points. And in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton beat Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, succeeding Republican Mike DeWine. Republicans entered Tuesday’s midterms with a 26-24 advantage in governor’s offices, but that majority appeared to be at risk early Wednesday. Thirty-six gubernatorial contests were on the ballot this year. “This incredible milestone marks a new era of Democratic leadership in states across the country,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, chair of the Democratic Governors Association, said in a statement. “Democratic governors and the DGA pulled off this amazing turnaround by competing and winning everywhere, staying focused on the biggest issues impacting Americans every day, and always standing up for our values.” Democrats also held on to gubernatorial power in critical swing states. In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated GOP Rep. Tom Tiffany to succeed two-term Democrat Tony Evers. And in Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won re-election by more than 20 percentage points. Democratic candidates remain locked in tight races in Arizona, Nevada and Michigan early Wednesday. In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs led Republican Rep. Andy Biggs, while in Kansas, state Sen. Cindy Holscher was locked in a tight contest with Republican Ty Masterson. Despite Kansas’ history as a solidly Republican state, it has had a Democratic governor for the last eight years. In battleground Nevada, state Attorney General Aaron Ford is facing off against GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo.

articles.title: Record number of female governors elected
articles.summary: Voters in 15 states have elected female governors, setting a record as Democrats made sweeping gains in races up and down the ballot.
articles.body: Voters in 17 states have elected female governors, setting a record in Tuesday’s election as Democrats made sweeping gains in races up and down the ballot. With some governor’s races still unresolved, at least 10 Democratic women were projected to win their contests, and two Republican women — Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn — were projected to do the same. Democratic women made historic gains in battleground states for their party, with former public health official Amy Acton in Ohio and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa in Texas emerging victorious in races that were not initially expected to be competitive. In her victory speech, Hinojosa told her supporters: “I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day, a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas. But God had a plan, and the people of Texas had a plan, too.” Acton in Ohio, Hinojosa in Texas, Blackburn in Tennessee, Amy Klobuchar in Minnesota, Helena Foulkes in Rhode Island and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia picked up governorships currently held by men. Georgia voters led the historic night with an early victory for Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to former President Joe Biden, who will become the first Black female governor in U.S. history. In her victory speech Tuesday night, Bottoms quoted the 1971 song “If I Were Your Woman.” “Georgia, I have said over the past few days: If I were your woman,” she told supporters. “Well, now I am your woman, and here is what I will do: I will never, ever, ever stop loving you. Thank you, Georgia, for electing me as your governor.” In Maine, Hannah Pingree was projected to win the governor’s race, keeping a woman in the highest statewide office after Janet Mills’ two terms. Similarly, in Michigan, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson was projected to hold her state’s governor’s mansion in Democratic hands, succeeding Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. In Massachusetts, New York and Arizona, Maura Healey, Kathy Hochul and Katie Hobbs were re-elected. Several races — including those in Oregon and New Hampshire — remained uncalled after midnight ET. But those races also had two female major-party nominees competing. The previous record for female governors serving at once was 14, a mark that was reached briefly last year and achieved again and sustained in the next year, after Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, both Democrats, were sworn in following 2025 election wins.

articles.title: Troy Jackson defeats GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, padding Democrats’ majority
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after an embattled Graham Platner dropped out, flipped control of the Senate seat.
articles.body: Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, NBC News projects, padding the Senate majority his party won in the midterm elections. Collins was a top target as the only Republican representing a state Donald Trump lost two years ago, even though she has won re-election in Democratic-leaning Maine for decades. Jackson and his allies worked to tie Collins to Trump, who has never won Maine, amid his sinking approval ratings. And Jackson had only a few months to make his case, having become the Democratic nominee in late July after Graham Platner’s exit from the race amid a sexual assault allegation, which he denied. Follow live updates on the midterm elections “Sen. Collins votes with Trump 96% of the time. The billionaire class is who she’s been fighting for,” Jackson said at one of their debates. Collins has challenged that percentage. Collins, meanwhile, stressed that she was instrumental in bringing federal dollars to the state as chairwoman of the powerful Appropriations Committee. “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships,” Collins said in one of the debates, later adding, “I have secured $1.5 billion for 672 projects all over the state of Maine during the past five years.” But Jackson argued that Collins’ power had not served Mainers, suggesting she could have used her sway to block some of Trump’s major policies, like tariffs and the war with Iran. Jackson also slammed Collins for voting to advance Trump’s sweeping tax cut and spending package, known as the “big, beautiful bill,” although Collins ultimately voted against final passage because of the measure’s Medicaid cuts. “Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is. But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people in Maine need it,” Jackson said at a debate. Jackson also sought to make a working-class pitch as a former logger from northern Maine, and he was the first challenger from Collins’ home county to take her on. Both Collins and Jackson hail from Aroostook County, a remote area of the state. Republicans tried to undermine Jackson’s pitch by casting him as a career politician who raised taxes. Republicans also initially tried to tie Jackson to Platner, even though Jackson called on Platner to step aside as the nominee when the sexual assault allegation came to light. But, like Platner, Jackson staked out liberal positions, including support for “Medicare for All” and abolishing ICE. He campaigned with left-wing Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., in the closing weeks of the race. While Jackson is a staunch progressive today, he has evolved since he entered politics more than two decades ago. Jackson decided to run for office after he helped lead a logger blockade at the northern border in 1998 to protest the hiring of Canadian workers. In 2000, he ran unsuccessfully for the state House as a Republican, but he won a legislative seat as an independent in 2002. He later became a Democrat and went on to serve in the state Senate, including as the chamber’s president from 2018 to 2024. Representing a rural area of the state, Jackson held some conservative positions, particularly on abortion. But he has said he evolved on the issue when he learned more about how “not having abortion care could hold people back and hold them down economically.” While some of Jackson’s stances have evolved, his supporters say he has consistently kept his focus on supporting working-class Mainers, dating to his own hardscrabble upbringing in Allagash. Jackson has deep ties to many unions in the state, which helped him organize and capture the Senate nomination after he lost the primary for governor this year. Jackson was also helped by a political environment that strongly favored Democrats as voters voiced concerns about Trump and his policies. Collins had built a unique political brand in the state. In 2020, she won re-election by 9 percentage points even as Trump lost the state by 9 points that year. But this year, she could not overcome the strong gravitational pull of anti-Trump sentiment even as she tried to distance herself from Trump, who did endorse her re-election. Collins specifically criticized Trump’s trade war with bordering Canada. In 2021, she was one of seven Senate Republicans who voted to convict Trump during his impeachment trial after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. “I have opposed the president when I think he’s wrong, and I’ve supported him when I think that he’s right. And that independent approach has been the approach that I’ve always followed,” she told NBC News while she was campaigning over the summer. But it was not enough to persuade Mainers that she should return to the Senate, where she has served since 1997.

articles.title: Dems seize the Senate as blue tidal wave crashes deep into Trump country, topples GOP strongholds
articles.summary: Democrats reclaimed the Senate Tuesday by toppling GOP candidates across Trump country, with Chuck Schumer clinching five pickups in a midterm wave.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — Democrats pulled off a spectacular drubbing of Republicans to reclaim power in the Senate Tuesday night, even without every race up for grabs across the map being decided. Democrats’ reclaiming of the upper chamber means that Republicans’ near two-year control of the federal government since President Donald Trump’s meteoric return to power will come to an end in January when the 120th Congress gavels into session. And they did so by carving a blue gash deep into Trump country, toppling several candidates that the president handpicked in many races that, until the waning weeks of the midterm election cycle, appeared out of reach for Democrats. The wave started in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., easily beat Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and continued rolling through North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Texas, where Senator-elect Rep. James Talarico, currently a state senator, handed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton a historic and decisive defeat in the Lone Star State. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY "We just took back Texas," Talarico told a roaring crowd of supporters Tuesday night. As Tuesday rolled into Wednesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., had clinched five pickups already, eviscerating Republicans’ thin, 53-seat majority in the upper chamber. The wave could still continue into Tuesday and roil through the GOP, with major races still outstanding that could swing Democrats’ way before the midterms are through. Contests in Michigan, Minnesota and Alaska were still outstanding, but even if Democrats lose those races, they’ll still claim power in the Senate. VETERAN DEM OPERATIVE SAYS SUBPAR GOP CANDIDATES POISED TO HAND OVER SENATE MAJORITY And coupled with a majority in the House, that means that Trump’s agenda in Congress will likely grind to a complete halt. Blame among Republicans was already flying as the dust continued to settle election night, with Trump, the quality of candidates running in tight races, and the top Republican running the Senate’s campaign arm, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., coming under an immediate and harsh microscope. VETERAN DEM OPERATIVE SAYS SUBPAR GOP CANDIDATES POISED TO HAND OVER SENATE MAJORITY "When the NRSC Chairman loses his home state of SOUTH CAROLINA…," a GOP operative told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Whether Schumer will be the one to lead Senate Democrats, however, remains in the air. Many of the candidates that scored a ticket to Washington, D.C., have remained noncommittal, or outright refused, to support him, arguing that the Senate Democratic caucus needed generational change in leadership.

articles.title: Democrat Andrews' South Carolina midterm victory defies prediction markets odds
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Prediction markets notched their first high-profile miss of Tuesday's US midterm elections, as Democrat Annie Andrews ousted Re...
articles.body:
Annie Andrews campaigns in South Carolina

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Prediction markets notched their first high-profile miss of Tuesday's US midterm elections, as Democrat Annie Andrews ousted ‌Republican Darline Graham to unexpectedly win a US Senate seat in conservative ‌South Carolina.

Prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket had implied a 70% chance of Graham, the sister ​of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, winning that race as of late afternoon Tuesday.

Andrews, a pediatrician, is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in South Carolina in 28 years. Republican President Donald Trump carried South ‌Carolina by 18 percentage points ⁠just two years ago, and neither Democrats nor Republicans considered the race to be competitive until recent weeks.

The outcome ⁠of several other competitive Senate races that have drawn millions of dollars in election bets will be under scrutiny. Many of those races were trending as ​the markets ​implied, with Democrats claiming Senate seats ​in Texas and Ohio.

With more ‌than $1.48 billion wagered on Tuesday's US midterm elections, prediction markets are facing their biggest test yet of how reliably they can forecast political races amid growing scrutiny of their businesses.

The platforms rose to prominence in 2024 when they bucked traditional opinion polls in signaling Trump would win the presidency, and have ‌since amassed a global following among media ​outlets and investors.

Though the markets cite high ​accuracy rates in providing betting ​odds, some high-profile misses during the US primaries and in Brazil's ‌presidential election have shown they are ​fallible, and analysts ​will be scrutinizing their midterm performance.

Spokespeople for Kalshi and Polymarket did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Tuesday. The companies ​have previously said that ‌events priced at relatively low probabilities frequently happen and political ​upsets are no different.

(Reporting by Douglas Gillison and Michelle Price, editing ​by Deepa Babington and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs wins re-election over GOP Rep. Andy Biggs in Arizona
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Hobbs defeated Biggs for a second term, keeping the key battleground state governorship in Democratic hands.
articles.body: Democrat Katie Hobbs has won re-election as governor of Arizona, NBC News projects, defeating Republican Rep. Andy Biggs in the key battleground state. Hobbs ran as a moderate in a state that Donald Trump won by 5 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. She focused on issues such as border security and tax cuts, and she chose John Giles, a former Republican and former mayor of Mesa, as her running mate. “Whether you’re a Democrat, independent or Republican, if you believe in protecting our freedoms and putting Arizona first, we’re ready to fight for you,” she said in a video announcing Giles as her pick for lieutenant governor. Hobbs, who previously was the state secretary of state, also highlighted her differences from Trump’s policies, including the unpopular Iran war and tariffs, and she enacted a three-year pause on tax incentives for data centers. While Hobbs’ campaign touted her record of working across the aisle and said she had signed more than 900 pieces of bipartisan legislation, Biggs focused on the record number of vetoes she signed during her four years as governor. “She doesn’t give in on anything, pretty much,” Biggs told Fox News in October. “I’d be working with the Legislature, not against them.” Biggs, a former chair of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, also ripped Hobbs for refusing to debate him, which she said she would not do because it’s “political theater.” Hobbs, meanwhile, hammered Biggs for his support of Trump’s tariffs, votes against resolutions to end the Iran war and refusal to acknowledge Joe Biden as the winner of the 2020 presidential election. In 2022, Hobbs similarly defeated a Trump ally who did not publicly accept the results of the 2020 election. That year, she defeated Kari Lake by about 17,000 votes. (Lake also challenged Hobbs’ victory in court and lost.) And as in her race against Lake, Hobbs refused to debate Biggs. Pressed about Hobbs’ 2022 victory during his gubernatorial campaign, Biggs said that “every court has said she’s won” and that “she’s the governor.” “Andy Biggs won’t admit that I won in ’22 or that Trump lost in 2020, and I think that it is dangerous and wrong. Arizonans have paid the cost of this election denial for a long time, and we will continue to if Andy Biggs is in the governor’s chair,” Hobbs said on a local radio program in July. Asked at the debate Hobbs skipped in October whether he would accept the election results no matter the outcome this time, Biggs said: “Yeah, I will. I will accept the outcome.” He said he believes Arizona elections are more secure now than in 2020. “I think that there’s been so much improvement, and there will continue to be improvement, that I’m happy to certify the outcome of this election,” he said. Trump initially backed businesswoman Karrin Taylor Robson when she declared her candidacy in early 2025, but he also backed Biggs when he jumped into the race later in the year. Taylor Robson later dropped out, at which point Trump gave Biggs his “complete and total endorsement.”
